cards.q: How does the WHO define mental health?
cards.a:
• A state of **mental well-being** that enables people to:
• **cope** with the stresses of life
• **realise their abilities**
• **learn and work well**
• **contribute to their community**
• Has intrinsic and instrumental value and is a **basic human right**
cards.m: Cope – Realise – Work – Contribute: health is more than absence of disorder

cards.q: What is primary health care (WHO), and what are its three components?
cards.a:
• A **whole-of-society approach** that brings health and well-being services **closer to communities**
• **Integrated health services** across the life course
• **Multisectoral policy and action** on the broader determinants of health
• **Empowering** individuals, families and communities to take charge of their own health
cards.m: Services + Policy + People

cards.q: What is ‘mental health care in primary care’ and which six areas does it focus on?
cards.a:
• Delivery of mental health services at the **first point of contact**, holistic and patient-centred
• **Promotion** of mental health
• **Prevention** of mental disorders
• **Early identification and screening**
• **Assessment and treatment**
• **Follow-up and continuity of care**
• **Referral** to specialist services when needed
cards.m: Pro-Pre-Spot-Treat-Follow-Refer – the whole journey sits in the KK

cards.q: Why integrate mental health services into primary health care (WHO/WONCA)?
cards.a:
• **Reduces stigma** – care in a familiar, non-psychiatric setting
• Encourages the public to **seek treatment early**
• **Accessible and affordable**
• **Strengthens community** mental health services
• **Better health outcomes** and **continuous care**
• **Protects human rights** (avoids institutional care)
cards.m: STEAM-CH: Stigma down, Treat early, Easy access, Affordable, More community care, Continuity, Human rights

cards.q: Which groups of mental disorders are commonly seen in general practice?
cards.a:
• **Mood**: major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder
• **Anxiety**: GAD, PTSD, OCD (DSM-5 now classifies PTSD and OCD separately from anxiety disorders)
• **Psychosomatic** (somatic symptom) disorders
• **Substance and alcohol use** disorders
• **Neurocognitive**: dementia, Alzheimer disease
• Note: slide spells ‘psychomatic’; correct term is **psychosomatic**
cards.m: MASS-D: Mood, Anxiety, Somatic, Substance, Dementia

cards.q: According to NHMS 2023, how common is depression among Malaysian adults?
cards.a:
• About **4.6%** of adults aged 16 and above – roughly **1 million** Malaysians
• Most are **undiagnosed and untreated** – hence opportunistic screening in KK
• Depression and anxiety are the commonest mental disorders seen in primary care
cards.m: ‘One in a million’ – literally about one million adults

cards.q: Why does much mental illness in primary care go unrecognised?
cards.a:
• Patients present with **physical complaints** (fatigue, aches, poor sleep, multiple vague symptoms)
• **Stigma** – reluctance to mention mood
• Short consultations focused on chronic disease
• **Comorbidity**: depression is common in diabetes, stroke, cancer and chronic pain
• Fix: **screen high-risk groups** (PHQ-2/Whooley, PHQ-9, DASS)
cards.m: The ‘ticket of entry’ is often a body symptom

cards.q: Why is depression in chronic disease patients a two-way problem worth screening for?
cards.a:
• Depression worsens **adherence**, self-care and glycaemic/BP control
• It raises risk of **coronary disease, stroke** and mortality
• Chronic illness, pain and disability in turn **cause depression**
• Post-stroke depression ≈ **36%**; breast cancer ≈ **19%**
• Primary care sees both sides and can treat them together
cards.m: Body and mind share one clinic card

cards.q: Which Malaysian helplines can a KK doctor give to a distressed patient?
cards.a:
• **Talian HEAL 15555** – MOH psychosocial support line
• **Befrienders** – 24-hour emotional support (KL: 03-7627 2929)
• **Talian Kasih 15999** – JKM helpline (abuse, family crisis)
• Helplines **supplement**, never replace, a proper risk assessment and follow-up
cards.m: HEAL = 15555; Kasih = 15999

cards.q: What does the MOH Mental Healthcare Performance Report (2016) signal for primary care?
cards.a:
• Malaysia measures mental-health service **performance indicators** nationally
• Policy direction: shift care from mental institutions to **community and primary care**
• KK clinics provide **screening, treatment and follow-up** of stable patients, with hospital psychiatry for complex cases
• The family physician links the two levels
cards.m: Hospital for crises, KK for continuity

cards.q: Fear vs anxiety – what is the difference?
cards.a:
• **Fear** = emotional response to a **real or perceived imminent** threat (here and now)
• **Anxiety** = **anticipation of a future** threat
• Both are normal; a disorder exists when they are **excessive, persistent and impairing**
cards.m: Fear = ‘Now!’; Anxiety = ‘What if…?’

cards.q: Which seven anxiety disorders are listed in DSM-5 (and on the slides)?
cards.a:
• **Generalised** anxiety disorder
• **Separation** anxiety disorder
• **Social** anxiety disorder
• **Selective mutism**
• **Panic** disorder
• **Specific phobia**
• **Agoraphobia**
• Anxiety disorders are among the commonest disorders worldwide (≈470 million people in 2023 per slide)
cards.m: ‘GSS-SPSA’: Go See Sam, Sam Panics Seeing Agora

cards.q: What physical symptoms of anxiety commonly bring patients to a KK?
cards.a:
• **Autonomic**: palpitations, fast breathing, sweating, hot/cold flushes, dry mouth
• **Neuromuscular**: tremor, muscle tension, numbness/tingling of hands/feet
• **Chest pain**, shortness of breath, choking sensation, dizziness/faintness
• **GI**: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain
• Fatigue, restlessness, poor sleep
cards.m: Adrenaline in every system – think ‘sympathetic storm’

cards.q: What are the cognitive and behavioural symptoms of anxiety?
cards.a:
• **Cognitive**: worry something bad will happen, uncontrollable thoughts/rumination, fear of **losing control, dying or going crazy**
• **Behavioural**: inability to be still, **avoidance**, irritability, impatience, easily distracted
• Avoidance maintains anxiety – it is the target of exposure therapy
cards.m: Think – Feel – Avoid: the anxiety loop

cards.q: Define generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) and its epidemiological associations.
cards.a:
• **Chronic, persistent, unrealistic, excessive worry** that interferes with daily activity
• Worry spans **many areas**: work, finances, family, health, everyday responsibilities
• **More common in women**
• Associated with **psychosocial stressors**
cards.m: GAD = ‘worry about everything, all the time’

cards.q: What is the DSM-5 duration criterion for GAD?
cards.a:
• Excessive anxiety and worry occurring **more days than not**
• For **at least 6 months**
• About **a number of events or activities** (not one single focus)
cards.m: GAD: 6 months of worry – ‘half a year of what-ifs’

cards.q: Which six associated symptoms are used for GAD, and how many are needed?
cards.a:
• **Restlessness** / feeling on edge
• **Easily fatigued**
• **Difficulty concentrating** / mind going blank
• **Irritability**
• **Muscle tension**
• **Sleep disturbance**
• Adults need **≥3 of 6**; children need only **1**
cards.m: ‘Worried RFCIMS’ – Restless, Fatigued, Concentration, Irritable, Muscles, Sleep

cards.q: Apart from duration and symptoms, what else is required to diagnose GAD (DSM-5)?
cards.a:
• The person finds the worry **difficult to control**
• Causes **clinically significant distress or impairment**
• **Not due to a substance** (caffeine, stimulants, withdrawal) or **medical condition** (e.g. hyperthyroidism)
• **Not better explained** by another disorder (panic, social anxiety, OCD, PTSD, illness anxiety)
cards.m: Uncontrollable + Impairing + not Substance/Medical + not another disorder

cards.q: Which medical and drug causes must be excluded in a patient presenting with anxiety?
cards.a:
• **Hyperthyroidism** – TFT
• **Arrhythmia** (SVT, AF) – ECG
• **Hypoglycaemia** – capillary glucose
• **Phaeochromocytoma**, asthma/COPD, anaemia
• **Caffeine, stimulants, salbutamol, steroids**; alcohol or benzodiazepine **withdrawal**
cards.m: THAW: Thyroid, Heart, ‘A’ low sugar, Withdrawal/drugs

cards.q: What is the GAD-7 and how is it scored?
cards.a:
• **7-item** self-report questionnaire (Spitzer et al., 2006) for GAD
• Asks about the **past 2 weeks**
• Each item scored **0–3** (not at all → nearly every day)
• Total **0–21**
• Screens for and grades severity of anxiety; not diagnostic on its own
cards.m: GAD-7: 7 items × max 3 = 21

cards.q: What are the GAD-7 severity bands and the usual cut-off?
cards.a:
• **0–4** minimal
• **5–9** mild
• **10–14** moderate
• **15–21** severe
• **≥10** = usual cut-off for probable GAD → clinical assessment
cards.m: 5-10-15 – same steps as PHQ-9 (which adds 20)

cards.q: What is the GAD-2 and when is it positive?
cards.a:
• The **first two items** of GAD-7: feeling nervous/anxious/on edge; not being able to stop or control worrying
• Score 0–6
• **≥3** = positive → complete the **full GAD-7** and a clinical assessment
cards.m: GAD-2 ≥3 and PHQ-2 ≥3 – the ‘rule of 3’ for two-item screens

cards.q: Has the GAD-7 been validated for use in Malaysian primary care?
cards.a:
• Yes – a **Malay version** was validated among **women attending a Malaysian primary care clinic** (Mohd Sidik, Arroll & Goodyear-Smith, 2012)
• Supports its use in **KK** settings for screening anxiety
cards.m: Local tool, local patients

cards.q: What is the first step in managing GAD (psychoeducation and lifestyle)?
cards.a:
• **Explain the nature of anxiety** and reassure
• **Sleep hygiene**
• **Regular exercise**
• **Reduce caffeine/stimulants**
• **Stress management**
cards.m: Explain – Sleep – Sweat – Skip the coffee – Stress-manage

cards.q: What psychological therapies are used for GAD?
cards.a:
• **CBT – first-line psychological treatment**
• **Applied relaxation**
• **Guided self-help / psychoeducation** for milder cases
cards.m: Mild → self-help; established GAD → CBT

cards.q: What is the drug treatment of GAD?
cards.a:
• **SSRI first-line** if medication is required (e.g. escitalopram, sertraline)
• **Alternative SSRI or an SNRI** if inadequate response or intolerance
• **Medication + CBT** in selected or severe cases
• Pregabalin if SSRIs/SNRIs are unsuitable; benzodiazepines only short term
cards.m: SSRI → switch SSRI/SNRI → combine with CBT

cards.q: How do you distinguish GAD from normal everyday worry?
cards.a:
• GAD worry is **excessive** (out of proportion to the actual risk)
• **Difficult to control**
• Spans **multiple domains**, jumping from topic to topic
• Present **more days than not for ≥6 months**
• Causes **distress or functional impairment** and physical symptoms
cards.m: Normal worry solves problems; GAD worry just spins

cards.q: Which comorbidities should you look for in a patient with GAD?
cards.a:
• **Depression** – very common; screen with **PHQ-9**
• Other anxiety disorders (panic, social anxiety)
• **Alcohol or sedative misuse** (self-medication)
• **Suicide risk** if depressed
• Comorbidity worsens prognosis and changes management
cards.m: Anxiety and depression are ‘twins who rarely travel alone’

cards.q: GAD vs panic disorder – what is the key difference?
cards.a:
• **GAD**: continuous, free-floating **worry** about many things; background tension
• **Panic disorder**: **discrete attacks** peaking within minutes, then **fear of further attacks**
• Both may coexist
cards.m: GAD = steady drizzle; panic = sudden thunderstorm

cards.q: Define separation anxiety disorder.
cards.a:
• **Fear or anxiety out of proportion** to the situation concerning **separation** from, or **abandonment** by, close **attachment figures**
• Attachment figures: **parents, partners** or other major attachment figures
• Can occur in **children and adults**
cards.m: ‘Don’t leave me’ disorder

cards.q: What are the risk factors for separation anxiety disorder?
cards.a:
• **Female** sex
• **History of childhood adversities**
• **Lifetime traumatic events**
• (Also: parental overprotection, family history of anxiety, life changes such as moving house or a parent’s new job)
cards.m: F-A-T: Female, Adversity, Trauma

cards.q: What are the clinical features of separation anxiety disorder?
cards.a:
• **Fear of losing or being separated** from attachment figures
• **Nightmares** about separation
• **Physical symptoms** of distress (headache, abdominal pain)
• **Excessive distress** when separation occurs or is **anticipated**
• **Persistent worry** about an unexpected event leading to separation (kidnapping, accident)
cards.m: Fear, Nightmares, Body aches, Distress, Worry

cards.q: What duration is needed to diagnose separation anxiety disorder in children vs adults?
cards.a:
• **Children and adolescents: ≥4 weeks**
• **Adults: typically ≥6 months**
• Fear must be **developmentally inappropriate** and cause impairment
cards.m: Kids – 4 weeks; grown-ups – 6 months

cards.q: When is separation anxiety normal in a child?
cards.a:
• **Normal developmental** separation anxiety appears around **8–10 months**, peaks at about **12–18 months**, and usually fades by **3 years**
• Crying when the parent leaves a toddler is expected
• Disorder = **developmentally inappropriate**, excessive and impairing (e.g. a school-age child refusing school)
cards.m: Toddler tears = normal; schoolchild school refusal = look closer

cards.q: How does separation anxiety commonly present to a KK in a school-age child?
cards.a:
• **School refusal**
• **Somatic complaints** (abdominal pain, headache, nausea) on **school mornings**, resolving at weekends/holidays
• Clinging, following the parent around the house, reluctance to sleep alone
• Always exclude organic causes and **bullying or abuse** at school
cards.m: Monday-morning tummy ache that vanishes by Saturday

cards.q: What psychoeducation and lifestyle measures are used in separation anxiety disorder?
cards.a:
• Involve **child + parents/caregivers**
• Explain the condition; avoid reinforcing avoidance
• **Encourage normal, age-appropriate activities** (school, sleepovers)
cards.m: Keep life normal – avoidance feeds anxiety

cards.q: What psychological therapy is used for separation anxiety disorder?
cards.a:
• **CBT ± gradual exposure** to separation
• **Reduce avoidance**
• **Parent/family involvement**
• **School collaboration** when required
cards.m: Graded goodbyes: small separations, growing steps

cards.q: When is medication used in separation anxiety disorder?
cards.a:
• **SSRI may be considered** for **moderate–severe** symptoms
• Consider **CBT + SSRI** in **severe or persistent** cases
• Psychological therapy remains the foundation
cards.m: CBT first; SSRI as the add-on for the stubborn cases

cards.q: Define social anxiety disorder.
cards.a:
• **Persistent anxiety about social situations**
• Leads to **significant distress** in performing routine tasks and **problems in interpersonal relationships**
• Fear, anxiety or avoidance is persistent, typically **≥6 months**
cards.m: Social anxiety = fear of the audience

cards.q: What symptoms occur in social anxiety disorder?
cards.a:
• **Shakiness/trembling**, **sweating**, **dry mouth**
• **Rapid heartbeat**
• **Tripping over the tongue** or unable to say words clearly
• **Stomach discomfort, diarrhoea**
• Often **blushing** – which the patient fears others will notice
cards.m: Shaky voice, sweaty palms, racing heart in front of people

cards.q: What are the diagnostic requirements for social anxiety disorder?
cards.a:
• Fear is **disproportionate to the actual threat**
• Typically persists **≥6 months**
• Causes **significant functional impairment**
• Core fear: **scrutiny and negative evaluation** (being humiliated, embarrassed or rejected)
• Feared situations are **avoided or endured with intense distress**
cards.m: Disproportionate + 6 months + Impairment

cards.q: What is the core fear in social anxiety disorder, and what is the ‘performance only’ specifier?
cards.a:
• Core fear: being **watched, judged and negatively evaluated** by others
• **Performance only**: fear restricted to **speaking or performing in public** (presentations, court, stage)
• Situational **propranolol** before the event may help this subtype
cards.m: ‘Everyone is looking at me’

cards.q: Social anxiety disorder vs normal shyness – how do you tell them apart?
cards.a:
• **Shyness**: a temperament; uncomfortable at first but **still participates**, no major distress
• **Social anxiety disorder**: **intense fear**, **avoidance**, physical symptoms, **≥6 months** and **functional impairment** (skips class, refuses jobs, no friends)
• Impairment is the dividing line
cards.m: Shy people still go to the party; socially anxious people stay home

cards.q: What is the first-line psychological treatment for social anxiety disorder?
cards.a:
• **Individual CBT – first-line**
• **Cognitive restructuring** of beliefs about being judged
• **Graduated exposure** to feared social situations
• **Social skills training** when appropriate
• Note: the slide lists these under a ‘psychoeducation & lifestyle’ heading – they are psychological therapies
cards.m: Rethink, then rehearse: restructure → expose → practise

cards.q: What general measures are part of managing social anxiety disorder?
cards.a:
• **Psychoeducation** about the anxiety cycle
• **Address avoidance** (avoidance keeps fear alive)
• **Treat comorbid depression or substance misuse** (alcohol is often used to cope in social settings)
cards.m: Look for the drink before the party

cards.q: What is the drug treatment of social anxiety disorder?
cards.a:
• **SSRI** if medication is required
• **SNRI** (e.g. venlafaxine) may be considered if inadequate response
• **CBT + medication** if partial response or severe symptoms
• Propranolol only for **performance-only** symptoms; not for generalised social anxiety
cards.m: Same ladder as GAD: SSRI → SNRI → combine with CBT

cards.q: Define selective mutism.
cards.a:
• A **childhood** anxiety disorder
• **Consistent failure to speak** in specific social situations where speech is expected (e.g. **school**)
• **Despite speaking normally in other situations** (e.g. at home)
• Usually begins in **childhood**
cards.m: Chatterbox at home, silent at school

cards.q: What duration and impairment criteria apply to selective mutism?
cards.a:
• Must **interfere** with educational achievement, occupational functioning or social communication
• Persist **at least 1 month**
• **Not limited to the first month of school** (silence while settling in is common)
cards.m: 1 month – but the first month of school does not count

cards.q: What associated features are seen in selective mutism?
cards.a:
• **Excessive shyness**, **fear of embarrassment**
• **Social isolation**, lack of social communication
• **Clinging to caregivers**
• **Temper tantrums** (often at home)
• **Impaired academic performance**
• Frequently comorbid with **social anxiety disorder**
cards.m: Shy, Silent, Sticky (clinging), Stormy (tantrums)

cards.q: What conditions must be excluded before diagnosing selective mutism?
cards.a:
• **Lack of knowledge of the spoken language** (e.g. new migrant, a child taught in a new language)
• **Communication disorder** (e.g. stuttering/fluency disorder)
• **Autism spectrum disorder**, intellectual disability, psychosis
• **Hearing impairment** – check hearing
• The child must speak normally elsewhere
cards.m: Can’t speak (language, hearing, ASD) vs won’t speak here (mutism)

cards.q: How is selective mutism managed?
cards.a:
• **Behavioural/CBT approaches – first-line**: **gradual exposure, stimulus fading, shaping, positive reinforcement**
• **Multidisciplinary**: child + parents, school/teachers, mental health professional, **speech-language therapist** when indicated
• **SSRI** may be considered for **severe/refractory** anxiety
cards.m: Fade in, shape up, praise often

cards.q: What is a panic attack?
cards.a:
• An **episodic surge of intense fear or discomfort**
• Usually **unexpected**, though sometimes a trigger is identifiable
• **Peaks within minutes** (slide: within 10 minutes) and **rarely lasts >30 minutes**
• Can occur within any anxiety disorder, depression or medical illness
cards.m: Rapid rise, rapid fall – a wave, not a tide

cards.q: How many symptoms define a panic attack (DSM-5), and which are they?
cards.a:
• **≥4 of 13** symptoms
• Cardiorespiratory: **palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath, choking**
• Autonomic: **sweating, trembling, chills/heat**, nausea, dizziness
• **Paraesthesia**, **derealisation/depersonalisation**
• Cognitive: **fear of losing control/going crazy**, **fear of dying**
• Note: slide says ‘one of the following’; DSM-5 requires **four**
cards.m: Fewer than 4 = limited-symptom attack

cards.q: What are the DSM-5 criteria for panic disorder?
cards.a:
• **Recurrent unexpected** panic attacks
• At least one attack followed by **≥1 month** of:
• **persistent concern/worry** about further attacks or their consequences, and/or
• **maladaptive behaviour change** (e.g. avoiding exercise or places)
• Not due to substance/medical condition
• Note: slide states ‘attacks for at least 1 month’; the 1 month refers to **worry or behaviour change after an attack**
cards.m: Panic disorder = fear of the fear

cards.q: What is the cognitive model of panic?
cards.a:
• **Catastrophic misinterpretation** of normal bodily sensations
• Palpitations → ‘heart attack’; dizziness → ‘I’m going to collapse’
• Interpretation → more fear → more adrenaline → more symptoms (vicious cycle)
• CBT breaks the cycle by testing these beliefs
cards.m: Heartbeat → ‘I’m dying’ → faster heartbeat

cards.q: Which medical conditions mimic a panic attack and must be excluded?
cards.a:
• **Cardiac**: arrhythmia (SVT), **ACS**, mitral valve prolapse
• **Endocrine**: **hyperthyroidism**, **hypoglycaemia**, phaeochromocytoma
• **Respiratory**: asthma, pulmonary embolism
• **Drugs**: caffeine, amphetamines, salbutamol; alcohol/benzodiazepine **withdrawal**
• Vestibular disorders, temporal lobe epilepsy
cards.m: Rule out the heart, the thyroid and the sugar first

cards.q: What investigations are reasonable in a KK for a first suspected panic attack?
cards.a:
• **12-lead ECG** (arrhythmia, ischaemia)
• **Capillary blood glucose**
• **TFT**, FBC
• Consider **urine drug screen** if stimulant use suspected
• Older patients or those with cardiac risk factors: treat as **chest pain** until ACS excluded
cards.m: ECG, glucose, thyroid – then diagnose panic

cards.q: How is an acute panic attack managed?
cards.a:
• **Reassure** and provide a **calm environment**
• **Controlled (slow) breathing**
• **Exclude important medical causes** when appropriate
• Avoid paper-bag rebreathing (risk of hypoxia if the cause is cardiac or respiratory)
cards.m: Calm room, slow breath, check the body

cards.q: Why do patients get tingling and carpopedal spasm during a panic attack?
cards.a:
• **Hyperventilation** → CO₂ blown off → **hypocapnia**
• **Respiratory alkalosis** → more calcium binds albumin → **low ionised calcium**
• Causes **perioral and fingertip tingling**, **carpopedal spasm**, dizziness, chest tightness
• Slow breathing reverses it
cards.m: Blow off CO₂ → alkalosis → ‘pins and needles’

cards.q: What is the long-term psychological treatment of panic disorder?
cards.a:
• **CBT**
• **Cognitive restructuring** of catastrophic interpretations
• **Interoceptive exposure**
• **Exposure to avoided situations**
cards.m: Change the thought, face the sensation, return to the place

cards.q: What is interoceptive exposure?
cards.a:
• Deliberately **inducing the feared bodily sensations** in a safe setting
• e.g. spinning in a chair (dizziness), running on the spot (palpitations), over-breathing
• Teaches the patient that the sensations are **harmless** – extinguishes the fear response
• A key CBT technique for **panic disorder**
cards.m: Make the heart race on purpose – and survive

cards.q: What is the drug treatment of panic disorder?
cards.a:
• **SSRI – first-line medication**
• **SNRI** may be considered
• **Avoid long-term benzodiazepines**
• Persistent symptoms → **reassess diagnosis and comorbidity**
• **Specialist referral** if refractory
cards.m: SSRI yes, benzo no (long term)

cards.q: Why start an SSRI at a low dose in panic disorder?
cards.a:
• SSRIs can cause **early activation/jitteriness** in the first 1–2 weeks
• Patients with panic are hypersensitive to bodily sensations and may stop treatment
• **Start low, go slow** (e.g. sertraline 25 mg, escitalopram 5 mg) and titrate
• Warn that benefit takes **2–4 weeks or more**
cards.m: Panic patients feel every milligram

cards.q: What should you do when panic symptoms persist despite treatment?
cards.a:
• **Reassess the diagnosis** (missed medical cause, e.g. thyroid, arrhythmia)
• Look for **comorbidity**: depression, substance misuse, other anxiety disorder
• Check **adherence** and adequacy of dose/duration
• **Refer to specialist** if refractory
cards.m: Not better? Re-diagnose before you re-dose

cards.q: Define specific phobia.
cards.a:
• **Irrational fear** towards **one (or more) specific object or situation**
• Leads to **impairment in daily function**
• Fear is out of proportion; object/situation is **avoided** or endured with intense anxiety
• Typically lasts **≥6 months**
cards.m: One trigger, one fear, total avoidance

cards.q: What symptoms occur on exposure to the phobic stimulus?
cards.a:
• **Panic attack**
• **Shaking/trembling**, **sweating**, **dry mouth**
• **Racing heartbeat**
• **Stuttering**
• **Tummy aches, diarrhoea**
cards.m: A cued panic attack

cards.q: What are the five DSM-5 subtypes of specific phobia?
cards.a:
• **Animal** (dogs, snakes, spiders)
• **Natural environment** (heights, storms, water)
• **Blood–injection–injury** (needles, blood, procedures)
• **Situational** (lifts, aeroplanes, enclosed spaces)
• **Other** (choking, vomiting, loud sounds)
cards.m: A-N-B-S-O: ‘A Nervous Boy Sees Others’

cards.q: What is unique about blood–injection–injury phobia?
cards.a:
• Causes a **vasovagal (biphasic) response**: brief tachycardia then **bradycardia and hypotension → fainting**
• Other phobias raise HR and BP without fainting
• Treated with **applied tension** (tensing large muscles to raise BP) plus graded exposure
• Relevant for blood taking, vaccination and insulin initiation
cards.m: The only phobia that makes you faint – so tense, don’t relax

cards.q: How is specific phobia treated?
cards.a:
• **Responds well to CBT**
• **Gradual (systematic) desensitisation** / graded exposure – treatment of choice
• Medication has a **limited** role (occasional short-term use for a rare unavoidable exposure, e.g. a flight)
cards.m: Face the fear in small steps

cards.q: Systematic desensitisation vs flooding – what is the difference?
cards.a:
• **Systematic desensitisation**: build a **fear hierarchy**, teach **relaxation**, then expose **step by step** from least to most feared
• **Flooding**: **immediate, prolonged exposure** to the most feared stimulus until anxiety subsides
• Both are behavioural techniques; desensitisation is better tolerated
cards.m: Staircase vs jumping in the deep end

cards.q: Define agoraphobia (and correct the slide’s classification).
cards.a:
• Fear of being in places where **escape might be difficult** or **help unavailable** if panic-like symptoms occur – especially unfamiliar environments
• Fear, anxiety or avoidance typically lasts **≥6 months**
• Note: slide calls it ‘a subtype of panic disorder’; since **DSM-5** agoraphobia is a **separate diagnosis** that may coexist with panic disorder
cards.m: Agora = marketplace: fear of being trapped in public

cards.q: Which five situations are listed in DSM-5 for agoraphobia, and how many are needed?
cards.a:
• **Public transport** (bus, LRT, plane)
• **Open spaces** (car parks, markets, bridges)
• **Enclosed spaces** (shops, cinemas)
• **Queues or crowds**
• **Being outside the home alone**
• Need fear of **≥2 of 5** (fear of only one = specific phobia, situational type)
cards.m: TOE-CO: Transport, Open, Enclosed, Crowds, Out alone – two or more

cards.q: How is agoraphobia treated?
cards.a:
• **Cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT)** with graded exposure
• **Supportive psychotherapy**
• **Insight-oriented psychotherapy**
• **Virtual reality therapy (VRT)**
• SSRI if comorbid panic disorder or severe
cards.m: CBT + VR: practise the mall before going to the mall

cards.q: Agoraphobia vs social anxiety vs specific phobia – what is the patient actually afraid of?
cards.a:
• **Agoraphobia**: being **trapped or unable to get help** if panic strikes (≥2 types of situation)
• **Social anxiety**: being **judged or humiliated** by others
• **Specific phobia**: the **object/situation itself** (dog bite, lift falling)
• Ask: ‘What do you think would happen?’
cards.m: Trapped vs Judged vs Harmed

cards.q: What do the slides mean by ‘5 major phobias’, and which are commonest?
cards.a:
• Phobias are grouped into the **five DSM-5 types** (animal, natural environment, blood–injection–injury, situational, other)
• Commonest specific phobias: **animals** (e.g. dogs, spiders), **heights**, **flying**, **enclosed spaces**, **needles**
• Most begin in **childhood**; more common in **females**
cards.m: Dogs, Drops (heights), Doors closed, Departures (flying), Darts (needles)

cards.q: What are the first-line drugs for anxiety disorders?
cards.a:
• **Modern antidepressants: SSRIs and SNRIs**
• **SSRIs**: **escitalopram**, **fluoxetine** (also sertraline, paroxetine)
• **SNRIs**: **duloxetine**, **venlafaxine**
• Onset of benefit **2–4 weeks**; full effect may take longer
cards.m: ‘Anti-depressants’ are really anti-anxiety first-liners

cards.q: What are benzodiazepines’ role and limits in anxiety disorders?
cards.a:
• **Second-line**, e.g. **alprazolam**, **clonazepam** (slide typo: ‘clonezepam’)
• Relax muscles and reduce **acute** anxiety quickly
• **Short-term only** because of **sedation, tolerance, dependence and withdrawal**
cards.m: Benzos are a bridge, not a home

cards.q: What are the safe-prescribing rules for benzodiazepines in primary care?
cards.a:
• **Lowest dose, shortest time – maximum 2–4 weeks**
• Avoid in the **elderly** (falls, confusion), **pregnancy**, **COPD/sleep apnoea**, history of **substance misuse**
• Avoid with **alcohol or opioids** (respiratory depression)
• Do not drive when sedated
• Long-term users: **gradual taper**, never stop abruptly (withdrawal seizures)
cards.m: 2–4 weeks, then taper

cards.q: What is buspirone’s place in anxiety treatment?
cards.a:
• A non-benzodiazepine **5-HT1A partial agonist** used in **chronic anxiety (GAD)**
• **No sedation, dependence or withdrawal**
• **Slow onset (2–4 weeks)** – useless for acute anxiety or panic attacks
• Not effective for panic disorder
cards.m: Buspirone = slow and safe; benzo = fast and risky

cards.q: When are beta-blockers used in anxiety, and when must they be avoided?
cards.a:
• Treat **physical symptoms** – severe **palpitations**, tremor (e.g. propranolol 10–40 mg)
• Useful for **performance anxiety**; do not treat the worry itself
• **Avoid in asthma** (bronchospasm), heart block/bradycardia, uncontrolled heart failure
• Mask hypoglycaemia warning signs in insulin-treated diabetes
cards.m: Propranolol quiets the body, not the mind – and never in asthma

cards.q: When is pregabalin used in anxiety, and what is its main caution?
cards.a:
• An **anticonvulsant** that **may be used for GAD when SSRIs and SNRIs are unsuitable** (intolerance, contraindication)
• Fast onset (about 1 week)
• Cautions: **dizziness, sedation, weight gain**, and **misuse/dependence** potential (now a controlled drug in many countries)
• Reduce dose in renal impairment
cards.m: Pregabalin = Plan B for GAD only

cards.q: How should you counsel a patient starting an SSRI for an anxiety disorder?
cards.a:
• Benefit begins after **2–4 weeks**; may take up to 6–12 weeks for full effect
• Early side effects: **nausea, headache, jitteriness, insomnia** – usually settle in 1–2 weeks
• **Sexual dysfunction** may persist – ask about it
• **Do not stop abruptly** (discontinuation symptoms)
• Continue about **12 months** after response to reduce relapse
cards.m: Slow to start, slow to stop

cards.q: How often should medication for an anxiety disorder be reviewed?
cards.a:
• Initially at **1–2 weeks**
• Then every **2–4 weeks for the first 3 months**
• Then **3-monthly**
• Each review: response, side effects, adherence, **suicidal thoughts**
cards.m: 1–2 weeks → 2–4 weekly × 3 months → 3-monthly

cards.q: What special precaution applies when starting an SSRI in a young person?
cards.a:
• Increased risk of **suicidal thoughts and self-harm** in the **early weeks**, especially under **25 years**
• Warn patient and family; give an emergency plan
• **Review within 1 week** of starting
• Avoid prescribing large quantities (overdose risk)
cards.m: Young + new SSRI = see them in a week

cards.q: What is the principle of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)?
cards.a:
• Thoughts, feelings and behaviours are linked
• CBT identifies **negative or panic-causing thoughts and behaviours** and turns them into **realistic, helpful ones**
• Uses **cognitive restructuring** and **behavioural experiments/exposure**
• Time-limited, structured, with homework
• **First-line psychological therapy** for most anxiety disorders
cards.m: Change the thought → change the feeling → change the behaviour

cards.q: What is biofeedback, and which other behavioural techniques are used for anxiety?
cards.a:
• **Biofeedback**: real-time display of a body signal (heart rate, muscle tension, skin conductance) so the patient learns to **lower it voluntarily**
• **Systematic desensitisation**: graded exposure with relaxation
• **Flooding**: prolonged maximal exposure
cards.m: See it, then control it

cards.q: Which relaxation techniques are recommended for anxiety disorders?
cards.a:
• **Progressive muscle relaxation** – tense then release muscle groups in sequence
• **Yoga**
• **Meditation**
• **Deep (diaphragmatic) breathing exercises**
• Cheap, safe, can be taught in a KK
cards.m: Tense-release, stretch, still the mind, slow the breath

cards.q: When should a patient with an anxiety disorder be referred to psychiatry?
cards.a:
• **Diagnostic uncertainty** or atypical features
• **Suicide risk**, self-harm or severe comorbid depression
• **Failure of ≥2 adequate treatments** (dose and duration)
• **Severe functional impairment**
• Comorbid **substance misuse, psychosis or bipolar disorder**
• Children with severe or persistent symptoms
cards.m: Doubt, Danger, Duds (failed drugs), Disability, Dual diagnosis

cards.q: What is the stepped-care model for anxiety disorders in primary care?
cards.a:
• **Step 1**: identification, **psychoeducation**, active monitoring
• **Step 2**: **low-intensity** interventions – guided self-help, psychoeducational groups
• **Step 3**: **high-intensity CBT/applied relaxation or drug treatment** (SSRI)
• **Step 4**: **specialist** care for refractory or high-risk cases
• Least intrusive effective treatment first
cards.m: Climb only as many steps as needed

cards.q: How does serotonin syndrome present, and what commonly causes it in primary care?
cards.a:
• Triad: **altered mental state** (agitation, confusion), **autonomic instability** (fever, sweating, tachycardia, diarrhoea), **neuromuscular hyperactivity** (**clonus**, hyperreflexia, tremor)
• Causes: SSRI/SNRI + **tramadol**, another antidepressant, St John’s wort, triptans, linezolid, MDMA
• Stop serotonergic drugs; refer to hospital if moderate/severe
cards.m: Clonus is the clue (NMS = rigidity and slow onset)

cards.q: How common is major depressive disorder in Malaysia and worldwide?
cards.a:
• **Malaysia**: studies show MDD prevalence of **8–12%**
• **Global** (meta-analysis): **4.7%**
• A common but complex illness with **varied symptom combinations**
cards.m: Malaysia 8–12 vs world 4.7

cards.q: What are the characteristic features of MDD, and what marks a more severe form?
cards.a:
• **Persistent low mood**, **loss of interest**
• **Poor concentration**, **sleep disturbance**, **fatigue**
• More severe: **functional impairment** and **suicidal ideation**
cards.m: Low mood + no joy + no energy

cards.q: How common is depression in primary care, and in which sex?
cards.a:
• Prevalence in primary care: **6.7–14.4%**
• **Women > men**
• Many present with physical rather than emotional complaints
cards.m: Roughly 1 in 10 KK attenders

cards.q: Which patient groups have particularly high depression prevalence (Malaysian CPG)?
cards.a:
• **Post-stroke**: **36%** (highest)
• **Postpartum women**: **20.7%**
• **Breast cancer**: **19.1%**
• **Elderly**: **6.3–18%**
cards.m: Stroke 36 > Postpartum 21 > Breast cancer 19 > Elderly up to 18

cards.q: Which high-risk individuals should be screened for depression in primary care?
cards.a:
• **First-degree relative** with depression
• **Chronic diseases**, **obesity**, **chronic pain** (headache, backache)
• **Pregnant/postpartum**, **old age**
• **Financial constraint**, impoverished home, **major life changes**, **socially isolated**
• **Multiple vague symptoms**, **sleep disturbance**, **substance abuse**, **loss of interest in sex**
cards.m: Family, Flesh (chronic disease/pain), Finances, Feelings hidden in vague symptoms

cards.q: Which screening tools for depression are listed in the Malaysian MDD CPG?
cards.a:
• **Whooley questions** (2 questions)
• **PHQ-9** (and PHQ-2)
• **DASS** (Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale)
• **HADS** (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale)
• **Beck Depression Inventory (BDI)**
• Positive screen → **clinical diagnostic assessment**
cards.m: W-P-D-H-B: ‘Why Patients Don’t Have Breakfast’

cards.q: What are the Whooley questions and how are they interpreted?
cards.a:
• Over the **past one month**, have you been bothered by:
• 1) **feeling down, depressed or hopeless**?
• 2) **little interest or pleasure in doing things**?
• **Yes to either** = positive → full assessment (PHQ-9 / clinical interview)
• Validated in **Malay** in primary care (with an added ‘help’ question)
cards.m: Two questions are as good as many

cards.q: How is the PHQ-9 structured and scored?
cards.a:
• **9 items** mirroring the **DSM-5** criteria for MDD
• Time frame: **past 2 weeks**
• Each item **0–3** (not at all / several days / more than half the days / nearly every day)
• Total **0–27**
cards.m: 9 DSM symptoms × 3 points = 27

cards.q: What are the PHQ-9 severity bands and the usual cut-off?
cards.a:
• **0–4** minimal
• **5–9** mild
• **10–14** moderate
• **15–19** moderately severe
• **20–27** severe
• **≥10** = usual cut-off for probable MDD
cards.m: 5-10-15-20: every 5 points climbs a step

cards.q: Why must PHQ-9 item 9 be checked separately from the total score?
cards.a:
• Item 9 = **thoughts that you would be better off dead or of hurting yourself**
• **Any score >0** requires a **direct suicide risk assessment at the same visit**, whatever the total
• A low total does **not** exclude risk
cards.m: Item 9 trumps the total

cards.q: What is the PHQ-2?
cards.a:
• The **first two PHQ-9 items**: little interest or pleasure; feeling down, depressed or hopeless
• **Past 2 weeks**, score 0–6
• **≥3** = positive → complete the PHQ-9 / clinical assessment
• Used as the first stage of two-stage screening
cards.m: PHQ-2 = Whooley with numbers

cards.q: What history should be taken when assessing a patient with suspected MDD?
cards.a:
• **Presenting symptoms**: onset, duration, severity
• **Past episodes**: number, severity, **treatment response**, **hospitalisations**
• **Suicide attempts**
• **Manic/hypomanic** episodes
• **Drug/alcohol abuse**; medical and drug history
• **Psychosocial stressors**, social support, occupation, **family history**
cards.m: Past, Present, Pills, Poles (mania), Plans (suicide), People (support)

cards.q: Why must you ask about mania or hypomania before starting an antidepressant?
cards.a:
• Depression may be the presenting phase of **bipolar disorder**
• An antidepressant alone may trigger a **switch into mania** or rapid cycling
• Missed bipolar disorder is a key cause of **non-response** (CPG)
• DSM-5 MDD requires **no history** of manic/hypomanic episodes
cards.m: Look up before you treat down

cards.q: What does the mental state examination evaluate in a patient with depression?
cards.a:
• **Severity** of depression (appearance, psychomotor change, affect, speech)
• **Psychotic symptoms** (mood-congruent delusions, hallucinations)
• **Risk of harm** to self and others
cards.m: MSE = Severity, Psychosis, Risk

cards.q: What is DSM-5 criterion A for a major depressive episode?
cards.a:
• **≥5 of 9 symptoms**
• Present during the same **2-week period**, a change from previous functioning
• **At least one** must be **depressed mood** or **loss of interest/pleasure**
• Nine: mood, interest, weight/appetite, sleep, psychomotor, fatigue, worthlessness/guilt, concentration, death/suicidal thoughts
cards.m: SIG E CAPS + mood: Sleep, Interest, Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor, Suicide

cards.q: How do the DSM-5 depression criteria differ for children and for weight change?
cards.a:
• In **children/adolescents**, mood can be **irritable** rather than sad
• Weight: **>5% change in a month** (loss when not dieting, or gain), or appetite change nearly every day
• In children: **failure to make expected weight gain**
• Psychomotor change must be **observable by others**
cards.m: Kids: cranky not crying; growth chart flat

cards.q: What are DSM-5 criteria B–E for major depressive disorder?
cards.a:
• **B**: clinically significant **distress or impairment**
• **C**: not due to a **substance or another medical condition**
• **D**: not better explained by **schizophrenia spectrum/psychotic disorders**
• **E**: **never a manic or hypomanic episode** (unless substance/medically induced)
cards.m: Impairment – no Substance – no Schizophrenia – no Mania

cards.q: How do you distinguish normal grief from a major depressive episode?
cards.a:
• **Grief**: sadness comes in **waves/pangs** linked to reminders; **self-esteem preserved**; humour and pleasure still possible
• **MDD**: **pervasive** low mood and anhedonia, **worthlessness, self-loathing**, suicidal ideation not just about joining the deceased, marked impairment
• DSM-5 allows MDD to be diagnosed alongside bereavement – use **clinical judgement and cultural norms**
cards.m: Grief: ‘I lost him.’ Depression: ‘I am worthless.’

cards.q: What should a suicide risk assessment in a KK cover?
cards.a:
• **Ideation**: frequency, intensity
• **Plan**: method, timing, **access to means**
• **Intent** and preparations (notes, giving away items)
• **Previous attempts**
• **Risk factors**: male, elderly, alone, alcohol, chronic illness, psychosis, hopelessness
• **Protective factors**: family, faith, children, future plans
• Asking directly does **not** increase risk
cards.m: IPIP: Ideas, Plan, Intent, Previous attempts – plus protection

cards.q: What are the three ICD-10 ‘typical’ symptoms of a depressive episode?
cards.a:
• **Depressed mood**
• **Loss of interest and enjoyment**
• **Reduced energy** (increased fatigability)
cards.m: Mood – Interest – Energy (MIE)

cards.q: What are the seven ICD-10 ‘common’ symptoms of a depressive episode?
cards.a:
• Reduced **concentration and attention**
• Reduced **self-esteem and self-confidence**
• Ideas of **guilt and unworthiness**
• **Bleak, pessimistic** views of the future
• Ideas or acts of **self-harm or suicide**
• **Disturbed sleep**
• **Diminished appetite**
cards.m: CoSt GuBS SA: Concentration, Self-esteem, Guilt, Bleak, Suicide, Sleep, Appetite

cards.q: How does ICD-10 grade the severity of a depressive episode?
cards.a:
• **Mild**: **2 typical + 2 common**; none intense; some difficulty with work/activities
• **Moderate**: **2 typical + 3 common**; some marked; considerable difficulty
• **Severe**: **all 3 typical + ≥4 common**; some severe; very unlikely to continue activities
• All need **≥2 weeks**
cards.m: 2+2 mild, 2+3 moderate, 3+4 severe

cards.q: When can a severe depressive episode be diagnosed with less than 2 weeks of symptoms?
cards.a:
• ICD-10 allows **<2 weeks** if symptoms are **very severe and of very rapid onset**
• Mild and moderate episodes always need **≥2 weeks**
cards.m: Severe and sudden can skip the 2-week wait

cards.q: Which organic causes of depression should be excluded, and with what tests?
cards.a:
• **Hypothyroidism** – TFT
• **Anaemia** – FBC
• Diabetes, renal/liver disease, **Cushing’s**, vitamin B12 deficiency
• Drugs: **corticosteroids**, isotretinoin, interferon, some antihypertensives; **alcohol**
• Neurological: stroke, Parkinson’s, dementia
• Missed organic causes are a reason for **non-response** (CPG)
cards.m: Check the thyroid and the blood before blaming the mind

cards.q: What are the risk factors for perinatal (antenatal) depression?
cards.a:
• **Socioeconomic disadvantage**
• **Unintended pregnancy**
• **Younger age**, **unmarried**
• **Hostile in-laws**
• **Intimate partner violence**
• **History of mental health problems**
cards.m: Poor, Young, Single, Unplanned, Abused, Past history

cards.q: What are the risk factors for postnatal depression?
cards.a:
• **Intimate partner violence** and **emotional violence**
• **Unplanned pregnancy**
• **Lack of support**
• **Partner’s use of alcohol**
• **Low-income household**
• (Also: past depression, previous postnatal depression)
cards.m: Violence, unplanned, unsupported, alcohol at home, low income

cards.q: How should perinatal depression be screened in a KK?
cards.a:
• **Two-stage approach**
• Stage 1: brief tool – **PHQ-2** or **Whooley questions**
• Stage 2: if positive → **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**
• Positive EPDS → clinical diagnosis by DSM criteria
cards.m: Two questions first, then ten (EPDS)

cards.q: What is the EPDS and what time frame does it cover?
cards.a:
• **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale** – **10-item** self-report scale
• Covers the **past 7 days**, not just today
• Each item 0–3; **maximum 30**
• Validated in **Malay** (Kelantan postnatal women)
• Can be used antenatally and postnatally
cards.m: EPDS: 10 items, 7 days, 30 points

cards.q: How is the EPDS scored?
cards.a:
• Items **1, 2 and 4** (no asterisk): top box **0** → bottom box **3**
• Items **3 and 5–10** (asterisked): **reverse scored** – top box **3** → bottom box **0**
• Sum all 10 items (max 30)
cards.m: 1, 2, 4 go straight; the rest are reversed

cards.q: What is the cut-off for the Malay version of the EPDS?
cards.a:
• **≥12** = positive screen (Malay version)
• → clinical assessment for depression
• Regardless of total, **any score >0 on item 10** (thoughts of self-harm) needs a **suicide risk assessment**
cards.m: Malay EPDS: 12 – a dozen

cards.q: How is depression in pregnant and postpartum women diagnosed?
cards.a:
• Use the **DSM-5 criteria for MDD** (≥5 of 9, ≥2 weeks)
• Add the specifier **‘with peripartum onset’** – onset **during pregnancy or within 4 weeks after delivery** (DSM-5)
• Grade as **mild, moderate or severe**
• Many clinical guidelines consider onset up to 12 months postpartum
cards.m: Same MDD criteria + a peripartum label

cards.q: Baby blues vs postnatal depression vs postpartum psychosis – how do they differ?
cards.a:
• **Baby blues**: up to **80%**; tearful, labile mood; **days 3–5**; resolves by **2 weeks**; reassure
• **Postnatal depression**: ≈**10–20%**; MDD features **≥2 weeks**, impaired functioning; treat
• **Postpartum psychosis**: ≈**1–2 per 1,000**; **first 2 weeks**; confusion, delusions, hallucinations; **emergency admission**
cards.m: Blues = brief; Depression = persistent; Psychosis = psychiatric emergency

cards.q: Why is postpartum psychosis an emergency, and what is the main risk factor?
cards.a:
• Risk of **suicide and infanticide**; rapid deterioration
• Features: insomnia, **confusion**, rapidly changing mood, **delusions about the baby**, hallucinations
• Main risk factors: **bipolar disorder** (personal or family) and previous postpartum psychosis
• Action: **same-day psychiatric admission**, ideally a mother-and-baby setting; never leave mother alone with baby
cards.m: Psychosis after birth = admit today

cards.q: Which antidepressants are preferred in breastfeeding and in pregnancy?
cards.a:
• **Breastfeeding**: **sertraline** preferred (low milk transfer, extensive safety data); paroxetine also low
• Avoid **doxepin** (infant sedation, respiratory depression); fluoxetine and citalopram give higher infant levels
• **Pregnancy**: sertraline commonly chosen; **avoid paroxetine** in the first trimester (cardiac malformations)
• Never stop an effective antidepressant abruptly on discovering pregnancy – weigh risks
cards.m: Sertraline for the ‘S’uckling baby

cards.q: How is perinatal depression treated in primary care?
cards.a:
• **Mild–moderate**: psychosocial support and **psychotherapy** (CBT, interpersonal therapy) first
• **Moderate–severe** or previous severe episodes: **antidepressant** after risk–benefit discussion
• Mobilise **family support**; screen for **intimate partner violence**
• Follow up closely; involve O&G, KK maternal health nurses and psychiatry as needed
cards.m: Talk first; tablets when moderate–severe

cards.q: Why does untreated perinatal depression matter beyond the mother?
cards.a:
• **Suicide** is a leading cause of maternal death in the first postpartum year
• Poor **mother–infant bonding**, early stopping of breastfeeding
• Infant **growth and developmental delay**, behavioural problems later
• Increased risk of **child neglect or abuse**
• Strain on the marriage and family
cards.m: Treat the mother, protect the child

cards.q: Why does depression in the elderly matter?
cards.a:
• **Higher morbidity and mortality**
• High levels of depressive symptoms predict developing **coronary artery disease, stroke** and combined disease
• Increased disability, poor self-care, non-adherence to treatment
• Highest suicide rates are in **older men**
cards.m: Sad heart, sick heart

cards.q: How does depression present in the elderly?
cards.a:
• **New-onset** or **recurrent** MDD
• **Psychomotor retardation**, **poor concentration**
• **Prominent anxiety** and **somatic symptoms** (aches, **constipation**)
• **Poor perceived health**
• **Cognitive deficits** – may mimic dementia
• Less likely to report sadness
cards.m: Old and slow, aching, anxious and forgetful – think depression

cards.q: Which screening tool is used for depression in the elderly?
cards.a:
• Mostly **self-rating scales**
• Commonest: **Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS)**
• **GDS-15**: yes/no questions; **≥5** suggests depression
• Avoids somatic items that overlap with physical illness
cards.m: GDS-15: 5 or more = depression likely

cards.q: What cautions apply when prescribing antidepressants to the elderly?
cards.a:
• **SSRIs**: **hyponatraemia (SIADH)** – check sodium; **GI bleeding** with aspirin/NSAIDs/anticoagulants; falls
• **Avoid TCAs**: anticholinergic effects (confusion, retention, constipation), **postural hypotension, falls, cardiotoxicity**
• Start low, go slow; review drug interactions
• Monitor **bone density** in osteoporosis risk
cards.m: Elderly on SSRI: check the salt and the bleeding

cards.q: What are the phases of MDD treatment and their aims?
cards.a:
• **Acute phase**: aim to **achieve remission**
• **Continuation and maintenance phase**: **prevent relapse, recurrence** and **development of chronicity**
cards.m: Acute = get well; continuation = stay well

cards.q: What is the acute treatment of mild-to-moderate MDD?
cards.a:
• **Psychosocial intervention** (support, problem solving, lifestyle)
• **Psychotherapy** (e.g. CBT, problem-solving therapy)
• **Pharmacotherapy** where indicated (e.g. patient preference, previous response, persisting symptoms)
cards.m: Mild–moderate: talk-based first, tablets as needed

cards.q: What is the acute treatment of moderate-to-severe MDD?
cards.a:
• **Pharmacotherapy** (antidepressant) – the main treatment
• Plus **psychotherapy** and **psychosocial intervention**
• **ECT** in selected severe cases
cards.m: Moderate–severe: tablets lead, talk supports

cards.q: How is MDD with psychotic features treated?
cards.a:
• **Pharmacotherapy**: antidepressant **plus an antipsychotic**
• **and/or ECT**
• Needs **specialist referral** – psychotic symptoms are a referral and admission criterion
cards.m: Psychotic depression: two drugs or the ‘electric’ option

cards.q: What are the indications for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) in depression?
cards.a:
• **Severe depression** with **psychotic features**
• **High suicide risk** needing rapid response
• **Refusal to eat or drink** / life-threatening self-neglect
• **Catatonia**
• **Treatment-resistant** depression, or previous good response to ECT
• Safe in pregnancy and the elderly when urgently needed
cards.m: ECT for the ‘too sick to wait’ patient

cards.q: Which drug classes are ‘second-generation antidepressants’ (Malaysian MDD CPG)?
cards.a:
• **SSRIs** (fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram)
• **SNRIs** (venlafaxine, duloxetine)
• **NaSSAs** (mirtazapine)
• **Melatonergic agonist and serotonergic antagonist** (agomelatine)
• **Multimodal** antidepressants (vortioxetine)
• **NDRIs** (bupropion)
• First step after diagnosis: **start a second-generation antidepressant**
cards.m: S-S-N-M-M-N: newer, safer than TCAs/MAOIs

cards.q: Which factors guide the choice of antidepressant?
cards.a:
• **Side-effect profile** (sedation, weight, sexual dysfunction)
• **Comorbidity**: cardiac disease → **sertraline**; insomnia/poor appetite → mirtazapine
• **Previous response** (own or family)
• **Drug interactions**, overdose safety (avoid TCAs if suicidal)
• Pregnancy/breastfeeding, **cost/availability**, patient preference
• In KK: **fluoxetine 20 mg** or **sertraline 50 mg** are common starts
cards.m: SCOPE: Side effects, Comorbidity, Overdose, Previous response, Expense

cards.q: When is response to an antidepressant assessed, and what if there is none?
cards.a:
• Assess response after **2–4 weeks**
• **No response** → **optimise** by titrating the dose as tolerated
• Reassess **after 2 weeks of optimisation**
• **Response** → continue to remission and then continuation/maintenance
cards.m: 2–4 weeks to judge, 2 more weeks after a dose rise

cards.q: What are the options if there is still no adequate response after dose optimisation?
cards.a:
• **Switch** to an antidepressant of a **different class**
• **Combination** of antidepressants
• **Augmentation** with **atypical antipsychotic, lithium or antiepileptic drug**
• **Consider referral to a psychiatrist**
cards.m: Switch – Combine – Augment – Refer

cards.q: What should be reconsidered when MDD does not respond to treatment?
cards.a:
• **Incorrect diagnosis** – e.g. missed **bipolar disorder**
• **Psychotic depression**
• **Organic conditions** – **anaemia, hypothyroidism**
• **Comorbid psychiatric disorder** – substance misuse, panic, OCD, personality disorder
• **Adverse psychosocial factors**
• **Non/poor compliance**
cards.m: DOPS-PC: Diagnosis, Organic, Psychosis, Substances/comorbidity, Psychosocial, Compliance

cards.q: How long should antidepressants be continued after remission (Malaysian CPG)?
cards.a:
• **6–9 months after onset of remission**
• **≥2 years** if there is a **high risk of relapse and recurrence** (e.g. recurrent episodes, residual symptoms, severe episodes)
• Then **taper gradually** over weeks
• Note: other guidelines quote 6–12 months; the slide (CPG) says 6–9 months
cards.m: First episode ≈ 6–9 months; recurrent ≈ 2 years or more

cards.q: Which antidepressants require BMI and waist circumference monitoring?
cards.a:
• **NaSSAs** (mirtazapine), **MAOIs**, **TCAs** – weight gain
• Frequency: **baseline and 6-monthly**
cards.m: Mirtazapine makes the waist grow

cards.q: Which antidepressants require blood pressure monitoring?
cards.a:
• **Venlafaxine** (dose-related **hypertension**)
• **TCAs** (postural hypotension)
• **MAOIs** (hypotension; hypertensive crisis with tyramine)
• At **baseline, after initial titration and at each dose change**; closer monitoring of MAOIs in the first weeks
cards.m: Venlafaxine pushes the pressure up

cards.q: When is an ECG for QT prolongation needed before or during antidepressant treatment?
cards.a:
• **TCAs**: at baseline in those **over 45 years** or with **cardiovascular disorders**
• **SSRIs/SNRIs**: at baseline in those with **CV risk** (citalopram/escitalopram are most QT-prolonging)
• **Sertraline** is the preferred SSRI in **ischaemic heart disease** (safety shown after MI)
cards.m: TCA + over 45 = ECG first

cards.q: What liver monitoring does agomelatine require?
cards.a:
• **LFTs** at **baseline, 3, 6, 12 and 24 weeks** after initiation
• Also after dose increases or when clinically indicated
• **Discontinue** if transaminases exceed **3 × upper limit of normal**
cards.m: Agomelatine: 3-6-12-24 weeks, stop at 3× ULN

cards.q: Which antidepressants cause hyponatraemia, and how should sodium be monitored?
cards.a:
• **SSRIs, mirtazapine, SNRIs, TCAs**
• Check electrolytes at **baseline and 1 month** after starting (or if clinically indicated) in **high-risk groups**
• More frequent monitoring in the elderly or existing hyponatraemia
• Mechanism: **SIADH**, with urine and serum osmolality
• Note: slide says ‘hypovolaemic’ hyponatraemia; SIADH causes **euvolaemic** hyponatraemia
cards.m: SSRI + old + thiazide = low sodium

cards.q: Who is at high risk of antidepressant-induced hyponatraemia?
cards.a:
• **Previous** antidepressant-induced hyponatraemia
• **Advanced age**
• **Low body weight**
• **Thiazide** diuretic use
• **Carbamazepine** use
cards.m: Past, Old, Thin, Thiazide, Tegretol

cards.q: When are a full blood count and bone mineral density monitored in antidepressant treatment?
cards.a:
• **FBC**: **mirtazapine, mianserin** – if clinically indicated, to detect **blood dyscrasias** (neutropenia, agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia), e.g. fever and sore throat
• **BMD**: **SSRIs** in those at high risk of **osteoporosis** – use the **FRAX** score (MOH Osteoporosis CPG)
cards.m: Mirtazapine + sore throat = FBC today

cards.q: What is antidepressant discontinuation syndrome and how is it prevented?
cards.a:
• Occurs on **abrupt stopping** (or missed doses), usually within 2–4 days
• Symptoms: **dizziness, ‘electric shock’ sensations, flu-like symptoms, insomnia, nausea, irritability, anxiety**
• Commonest with **paroxetine and venlafaxine** (short half-life); rare with fluoxetine
• Prevent by **tapering over ≥4 weeks**; not a sign of addiction
cards.m: FINISH: Flu-like, Insomnia, Nausea, Imbalance, Sensory (zaps), Hyperarousal

cards.q: What are the criteria for referring a patient with MDD to psychiatry?
cards.a:
• **Unsure of diagnosis**
• **Attempted suicide**; **active suicidal ideas**
• **Psychotic symptoms**
• **Failure of treatment**; need for **advice on further treatment**
• **Recurrent episode within one year**
• **Severe agitation**, **self-neglect**
• **Clinical deterioration**
cards.m: Doubt, Danger, Delusions, Duds, Déjà vu (recurrence), Decline

cards.q: What are the criteria for admitting a patient with MDD?
cards.a:
• **Risk of harm to self** (active suicidal plan, recent serious attempt)
• **Psychotic symptoms**
• **Inability to care for self** (e.g. not eating or drinking)
• **Lack of impulse control**
• **Danger to others**
• Admission may be voluntary or under the **Mental Health Act 2001**
cards.m: Self, Psychosis, Self-care, Impulse, Others

cards.q: How is psychosomatic (somatic symptom) disorder defined?
cards.a:
• **Physical symptoms are real and distressing**
• May occur **with or without** an identifiable medical disease
• Key problem: **excessive thoughts, anxiety or behaviours** related to the symptoms
• Causes **significant distress or functional impairment**
cards.m: The symptom is real; the reaction is excessive

cards.q: What are the common presentations of psychosomatic disorders in primary care?
cards.a:
• **Pain** (back, joints, abdomen)
• **Headache**
• **Fatigue/weakness**
• **Palpitations**
• **GI symptoms** (bloating, IBS-like)
• **Shortness of breath**
cards.m: Pain, Head, Tired, Heart, Gut, Breath

cards.q: What are the DSM-5 criteria for somatic symptom disorder?
cards.a:
• **≥1 distressing somatic symptom** causing significant disruption of daily life
• **Excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviours** about it, with **at least one** of:
• persistent **disproportionate thoughts** about seriousness
• persistently **high anxiety** about health/symptoms
• **excessive time and energy** devoted to symptoms
• **Persistent** – typically **>6 months** (individual symptoms may change)
cards.m: One symptom + one excess (Thoughts, Anxiety, Time)

cards.q: Is the absence of a medical explanation required to diagnose somatic symptom disorder?
cards.a:
• **No** – DSM-5 dropped ‘medically unexplained’ as a requirement
• Diagnosis rests on the **excessive psychological response** to symptoms
• It can coexist with real disease (e.g. a diabetic patient consumed by fear of every ache)
• This avoids implying symptoms are ‘fake’
cards.m: Diagnose the response, not the absence of disease

cards.q: What is the course of somatic symptom disorder?
cards.a:
• Generally **persistent** (typically >6 months)
• **Individual symptoms may change** over time while preoccupation continues
• Leads to **frequent attendance**, many investigations and ‘doctor shopping’
• Risk of **iatrogenic harm** from unnecessary tests and procedures
cards.m: The symptom moves; the worry stays

cards.q: Somatic symptom disorder vs illness anxiety disorder – what is the difference?
cards.a:
• **Somatic symptom disorder**: **prominent distressing symptoms** + excessive response
• **Illness anxiety disorder** (old ‘hypochondriasis’): **minimal or no symptoms**, but **preoccupation with having or getting a serious illness** for **≥6 months**; checking or avoidance behaviour
• Both: reassurance helps only briefly
cards.m: SSD = ‘my pain is terrible’; IAD = ‘I must have cancer’

cards.q: What is conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder)?
cards.a:
• **Neurological symptoms** (weakness, paralysis, non-epileptic seizures, blindness, aphonia) **incompatible with recognised disease**
• Positive signs: **Hoover’s sign**, give-way weakness, non-dermatomal sensory loss
• Often follows **psychological stress**; may show ‘la belle indifférence’
• **Not intentionally produced**
cards.m: Converts stress into a neurological sign

cards.q: Factitious disorder vs malingering – how do they differ?
cards.a:
• Both: symptoms are **intentionally produced or feigned**
• **Factitious disorder**: motive is **internal** – to assume the **sick role** (no obvious external reward); includes ‘imposed on another’ (e.g. a child)
• **Malingering**: motive is an **external incentive** – sick leave, compensation, avoiding duty, obtaining drugs
• Malingering is **not a mental disorder**
cards.m: Factitious = wants to be a patient; Malingering = wants the money

cards.q: How should a family physician manage somatic symptom disorder?
cards.a:
• **Acknowledge** symptoms as real; avoid ‘it’s all in your head’
• **Regular, brief, scheduled visits** with **one doctor** (not symptom-driven)
• **Limit investigations and referrals** to clear indications
• Focus on **function and coping** rather than cure
• Treat comorbid **depression/anxiety**; offer **CBT**
cards.m: Same doctor, set dates, sensible tests

cards.q: Which treatments help patients with somatic symptom disorder?
cards.a:
• **Explain the mind–body link** (stress amplifies real sensations) – ‘reattribution’
• **CBT** – best evidence
• **Graded activity/exercise**, relaxation, sleep hygiene
• **Antidepressants** (SSRI/SNRI; low-dose TCA for chronic pain) for comorbid depression, anxiety or pain
• Avoid opioids and benzodiazepines
cards.m: Explain, Exercise, CBT – not more scans

cards.q: Which red flags mean a ‘known somatiser’ needs fresh investigation?
cards.a:
• **New or changed** symptom pattern, especially after **age 50**
• **Weight loss**, night sweats, fever
• **Nocturnal** symptoms, bleeding, progressive neurological deficit
• **Objective abnormal signs** or abnormal results
• Patients with SSD can still develop organic disease – examine every time
cards.m: A somatiser can still get cancer

cards.q: What helps frequent attenders with medically unexplained symptoms in primary care?
cards.a:
• **Psychosomatic therapy** – body-oriented sessions (breathing, relaxation, physical activity, education on stress and symptoms) delivered by trained physiotherapists/exercise therapists, alongside the GP
• **Planned, regular GP reviews** with continuity
• **CBT** and collaborative care
• Goal: fewer visits and investigations, better function
cards.m: Frequent attenders need scheduled attention, not more tests

cards.q: Which comorbidities should be screened for in a patient with somatic symptom disorder?
cards.a:
• **Depression** – PHQ-9
• **Anxiety** – GAD-7, panic
• **Substance misuse** (analgesics, sedatives, alcohol)
• **Trauma/abuse** history, domestic violence
• Treating comorbidity often reduces somatic symptoms
cards.m: Look under the symptom for sadness and fear

cards.q: Define dementia.
cards.a:
• A **pathological syndrome** in which **cognitive function** (ability to process thought) **deteriorates progressively**
• Interferes with **independence in daily activities**
• It is **not part of normal ageing**
cards.m: Dementia is a disease, not a birthday

cards.q: How common is dementia among elderly Malaysians?
cards.a:
• **NHMS 2018 (Elderly Health)**: overall prevalence of **probable dementia = 8.5%**
• Rising with population ageing
• Many cases are undiagnosed in primary care
cards.m: 8.5% – nearly 1 in 12 older Malaysians

cards.q: What are the main causes of dementia?
cards.a:
• **Alzheimer disease – 60–70%** (commonest)
• **Vascular dementia**
• **Dementia with Lewy bodies**
• **Frontotemporal dementia**
• **Parkinson disease dementia**
• **Mixed dementia** (usually Alzheimer + vascular)
cards.m: All Very Lewd Folk Pick Mixtures

cards.q: What are the pathology and typical presentation of Alzheimer disease?
cards.a:
• Pathology: **amyloid-β plaques**, **neurofibrillary (tau) tangles**, loss of **cholinergic neurons**
• **Insidious onset**, **gradual progression**
• Early **short-term (episodic) memory loss** – repeats questions, misplaces items
• Later: language, visuospatial, executive and functional decline
• Main risk factor: **age**; also family history, Down syndrome
cards.m: Alzheimer’s starts with forgetting yesterday

cards.q: What are the features of vascular dementia?
cards.a:
• **Abrupt onset** or **stepwise deterioration**, often after strokes/TIAs
• **Vascular risk factors**: hypertension, diabetes, smoking, AF, dyslipidaemia
• **Focal neurological signs**, gait disturbance
• Early **executive dysfunction** and slowed thinking; memory may be relatively spared
• Prevention: control vascular risk factors
cards.m: Vascular = stairs going down; Alzheimer = a slope

cards.q: What are the core features of dementia with Lewy bodies, and how is it separated from Parkinson disease dementia?
cards.a:
• **Fluctuating cognition** and alertness
• **Recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations**
• **Parkinsonism**
• **REM sleep behaviour disorder**
• **Severe sensitivity to antipsychotics** (rigidity, falls, death)
• **1-year rule**: dementia before or within 1 year of parkinsonism = DLB; dementia >1 year after established Parkinson’s = PDD
cards.m: Lewy: Looks (hallucinations), Lapses (fluctuations), Limbs (parkinsonism)

cards.q: What are the features of frontotemporal dementia?
cards.a:
• **Younger onset** (often <65 years)
• Early **personality and behaviour change**: **disinhibition**, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsions, hyperorality
• Or early **language** impairment (primary progressive aphasia)
• **Memory relatively preserved** early
• Frequently misdiagnosed as a psychiatric illness
cards.m: Frontal = Front of personality changes first

cards.q: What are the steps of dementia assessment from primary care to referral?
cards.a:
• **Clinical assessment** – history, examination, cognitive screening
• **Laboratory tests** – exclude reversible mimics
• **Imaging** (CT/MRI)
• Apply **diagnostic criteria** (DSM-5)
• **Management and treatment** plan
cards.m: History → Bloods → Brain scan → Criteria → Care

cards.q: Why is a caregiver history essential in dementia assessment?
cards.a:
• Patients often **lack insight** and minimise problems
• Informant describes **onset, progression**, functional decline, behaviour change, safety issues
• Structured **dementia questionnaires** (e.g. AD8 informant interview) support the history
• Also assess **caregiver burden**
cards.m: The family remembers what the patient forgets

cards.q: Which cognitive screening tools are used in primary care, and what are their cut-offs?
cards.a:
• **MMSE** (30 points): **≤23/24** suggests impairment; adjust for low education
• **MoCA** (30 points): **<26** abnormal; **+1 point** if ≤12 years of education; more sensitive for **MCI** and executive dysfunction
• **Mini-Cog** (3-word recall + clock): **<3/5** positive
• **AD8** informant questionnaire: **≥2** positive
• Screening ≠ diagnosis
cards.m: MMSE 24, MoCA 26

cards.q: How is dementia severity graded on the MMSE?
cards.a:
• **Mild**: MMSE **21–26**
• **Moderate**: **10–20**
• **Severe**: **<10**
• Used with functional status to guide drug choice (AChEI mild–moderate; memantine moderate–severe)
cards.m: Twenty and ten split mild, moderate and severe

cards.q: Which dementia mimics are excluded by laboratory tests?
cards.a:
• **Hypothyroidism**
• **Vitamin B12 deficiency**
• **Hypercalcaemia**
• **Neurosyphilis**
• **HIV-related dementia**
cards.m: Thyroid, B12, Calcium, Syphilis, HIV – the ‘bloods that can bring memory back’

cards.q: What is the standard ‘reversible causes’ blood screen for new cognitive decline?
cards.a:
• **FBC**, renal profile and **electrolytes**, **calcium**
• **Glucose / HbA1c**
• **LFT**
• **TFT**
• **Vitamin B12 and folate**
• **VDRL/syphilis serology**; **HIV** if risk factors
• Plus urinalysis if delirium is suspected
cards.m: FBC, Salts, Sugar, Liver, Thyroid, B12/folate, Syphilis

cards.q: Which dementia mimics are excluded by imaging or EEG?
cards.a:
• **Normal pressure hydrocephalus**
• **Brain tumour**
• **Subdural haemorrhage** (elderly, falls, anticoagulants)
• **Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease** (EEG periodic complexes, MRI)
• **Autoimmune limbic encephalitis**
cards.m: Water, Tumour, Blood, Prion, Antibody

cards.q: What is normal pressure hydrocephalus and why is it important?
cards.a:
• Triad: **gait disturbance** (magnetic, broad-based), **urinary incontinence**, **dementia**
• CT/MRI: **ventriculomegaly** out of proportion to atrophy
• **Potentially reversible** with **ventriculoperitoneal shunting** – refer neurosurgery
• Gait usually improves most
cards.m: Wet, Wobbly, Wacky

cards.q: What is the role of imaging and biomarkers in dementia assessment?
cards.a:
• **CT/MRI brain**: exclude structural causes (tumour, subdural, NPH); show **vascular lesions** or **atrophy** (medial temporal/hippocampal in Alzheimer’s)
• **SPECT/PET**: perfusion or metabolism patterns; **DaT scan** for DLB
• **CSF** amyloid/tau and amyloid PET: specialist use
• Usually arranged via hospital/memory clinic referral
cards.m: Scan to exclude, then to characterise

cards.q: What are the DSM-5 criteria for major neurocognitive disorder (dementia)?
cards.a:
• **A**: **significant cognitive decline** from previous level in **one or more** cognitive domains
• **B**: deficits **interfere with independence** in everyday activities
• **C**: not exclusively during **delirium**
• **D**: not better explained by another mental disorder (e.g. depression, schizophrenia)
cards.m: Decline + Dependence – Delirium – Depression

cards.q: What is mild cognitive impairment (MCI)?
cards.a:
• **Modest cognitive decline** from previous level in one or more domains
• Deficits **do NOT interfere with independence** in everyday activities (may need more effort)
• Not exclusively in delirium; not better explained by another disorder
• About **10–15%/year** progress to dementia – review annually and control vascular risk
cards.m: MCI: memory slips, life intact

cards.q: How is dementia severity graded by functional status?
cards.a:
• **Mild**: difficulty with **instrumental ADLs** – housework, managing money, shopping, medications
• **Moderate**: difficulty with **basic ADLs** – feeding, dressing, bathing
• **Severe**: **fully dependent**
cards.m: Money first, then meals and clothes, then everything

cards.q: Dementia vs delirium – what are the key differences?
cards.a:
• **Delirium**: **acute** onset (hours–days), **fluctuating**, **inattention**, altered consciousness; usually a precipitant (infection, drugs, retention, hypoxia); often **reversible**
• **Dementia**: **insidious**, progressive over months–years; **alert**; attention preserved until late
• Dementia is the **biggest risk factor** for delirium – look for ‘acute on chronic’
• Screen with the **Confusion Assessment Method (CAM)**
cards.m: Delirium = sudden storm; dementia = slow sunset

cards.q: How do you distinguish depression with cognitive impairment (‘pseudodementia’) from dementia?
cards.a:
• **Depression**: **subacute** onset, often after a loss; patient **complains of poor memory**; **‘don’t know’ answers**, poor effort; low mood precedes memory problems; improves with antidepressant
• **Dementia**: insidious; patient **minimises** deficits, **near-miss** answers, confabulation; family notices first
• Screen with **GDS**; depression can also be an early sign of dementia
cards.m: Depressed patients say ‘I can’t remember’; dementia patients say ‘I’m fine’

cards.q: What are the first-line non-drug strategies for cognitive symptoms in dementia?
cards.a:
• First-line, especially in **mild-to-moderate** stages
• **Cognitive stimulation therapy** – group sessions to enhance memory and problem-solving
• **Physical activity** – improves cognition and mood
• **Occupational therapy** – maintains independence in daily living
cards.m: Think, Move, Do

cards.q: How are behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) managed without drugs?
cards.a:
• **Address underlying causes**: **pain, infection, sensory deficits** (and constipation, retention, drugs)
• **Calm environment**, **familiar routines**
• **Music or pet therapy**; tailored activities to reduce agitation/aggression
• **Family/caregiver education and support**
cards.m: Agitation is a message – look for pain first

cards.q: How do acetylcholinesterase inhibitors work, and which are used?
cards.a:
• **Increase acetylcholine** by preventing its breakdown
• Indicated for **mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease**
• **Donepezil** – once daily, used across stages
• **Rivastigmine** – oral or **patch**; also for **Parkinson disease dementia** (and DLB)
• **Galantamine** – the third AChEI
cards.m: Donepezil, Rivastigmine, Galantamine – ‘DRaG’ ACh back up

cards.q: What are the side effects and cautions of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors?
cards.a:
• **Cholinergic GI effects**: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, anorexia/weight loss
• **Bradycardia**, heart block, **syncope** – check pulse/ECG; caution with beta-blockers, sick sinus syndrome
• Vivid dreams/insomnia (give donepezil in the morning if so), muscle cramps
• Caution: **asthma/COPD**, peptic ulcer
cards.m: Too much ACh: slow heart, upset gut

cards.q: What is memantine and when is it used?
cards.a:
• **NMDA receptor antagonist** – reduces neuronal damage from excessive **glutamate**
• Indicated for **moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease**
• Can be used **alone or combined with an AChEI**
• Option when AChEIs are not tolerated or contraindicated (e.g. bradycardia)
cards.m: Memantine for More advanced disease

cards.q: When may antipsychotics be used in dementia, and why with caution?
cards.a:
• **Only if BPSD are severe or dangerous**: aggression, hallucinations or delusions posing safety risks
• **Short-term**, lowest dose, review and taper (e.g. every 6–12 weeks)
• Risks: **stroke**, **increased mortality**, sedation, falls, parkinsonism
• Examples: **risperidone**, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole
• **Avoid in Lewy body dementia** (severe sensitivity)
cards.m: Antipsychotics in dementia: last resort, least dose, least time

cards.q: Which drugs are used for depression and anxiety in dementia?
cards.a:
• **Antidepressants** for depression, anxiety or agitation – **SSRIs, e.g. sertraline**
• Note: slide lists **oxazepam** under antidepressants; oxazepam is a **benzodiazepine** – if used at all for anxiety, only short term, as benzodiazepines worsen confusion and falls
• Avoid TCAs (anticholinergic)
cards.m: SSRI yes; benzo only briefly

cards.q: Which medications worsen cognition and should be reviewed in a patient with dementia?
cards.a:
• **Anticholinergics**: oxybutynin, **chlorpheniramine**, TCAs (amitriptyline), hyoscine
• **Benzodiazepines** and **Z-drugs**
• Opioids, **antipsychotics**, some antiepileptics
• Check the **anticholinergic burden**; deprescribe where possible
• Anticholinergics also **oppose AChEIs**
cards.m: Every anticholinergic is an anti-memory drug

cards.q: How should the family physician support carers of people with dementia?
cards.a:
• **Educate** about the diagnosis, expected course and BPSD
• Screen for **carer stress, depression and burnout**; offer **respite** and day care
• Link with support groups (e.g. **Alzheimer’s Disease Foundation Malaysia**), JKM and community services
• Discuss **safety** (driving, wandering, cooking), **legal and financial planning** and **advance care planning** early
cards.m: Care for the carer, or you lose two patients

cards.q: How can we support people around us who are struggling with their mental health?
cards.a:
• **Listen without judgement**
• **Check on** friends and family regularly
• **Offer encouragement**
• **Respect their feelings**
• Help them reach professional help when needed
cards.m: Listen, Check in, Encourage, Respect

cards.q: How can the stigma of mental illness be broken?
cards.a:
• **Spread awareness** – education reduces misunderstanding
• **Stop judging others** – people deserve understanding, not criticism or negative labels
• Use **person-first language** (‘a person with depression’, not ‘a depressive’)
• Deliver care in **integrated, non-psychiatric settings** such as KK
cards.m: Educate, don’t label

cards.q: Give an example of primary, secondary and tertiary prevention for mental health in primary care.
cards.a:
• **Primary**: promote resilience – stress management, exercise, parenting programmes, school mental-health education, reducing alcohol/drug use
• **Secondary**: **early detection** – screening high-risk groups (PHQ-2/Whooley, EPDS, DASS) and early treatment
• **Tertiary**: **rehabilitation** and relapse prevention – adherence, follow-up, psychosocial and vocational rehabilitation
cards.m: Prevent – Detect – Rehabilitate

cards.q: What is the role of the family physician in mental health care?
cards.a:
• **First contact** and **gatekeeper**; recognises hidden distress
• **Screens** high-risk groups and **diagnoses** common disorders
• **Treats** mild–moderate depression and anxiety; **continuity** and follow-up
• **Coordinates referral** and shared care with psychiatry
