• Supports **families and carers**; manages the **physical health** of people with serious mental illness
cards.m: First contact, continuous, comprehensive, coordinated

cards.q: How should you respond when someone discloses suicidal thoughts?
cards.a:
• **Ask directly** about suicide – it does not plant the idea
• **Listen** calmly, without judgement or arguing
• **Do not leave them alone** if at immediate risk; **remove access to means**
• Connect to help: doctor, family, **Talian HEAL 15555**, Befrienders, emergency department (999)
• Follow up
cards.m: Ask, Listen, Stay, Remove, Refer

cards.q: Which lifestyle and social factors protect mental health?
cards.a:
• **Social connectedness** – ‘you are not alone’
• **Regular physical activity** and adequate **sleep**
• Avoiding **alcohol, smoking and drugs**
• **Healthy coping skills** and stress management; spiritual/religious support
• **Meaningful activity** – work, study, volunteering
cards.m: Connect, Move, Sleep, Abstain, Cope

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes attends a Klinik Kesihatan. His HbA1c has risen from 7.6% to 9.8% over a year, he has missed two appointments and says he is ‘just tired’ and sleeping badly since he retired. Examination is unremarkable.
What is the best next step?
o: Add bedtime basal insulin and review his HbA1c in three months
Refer to the dietitian for intensive carbohydrate counselling
Ask the two Whooley questions and complete a PHQ-9 if positive
Request TFT, FBC and morning cortisol before discussing mood
Refer to psychiatry for a formal diagnostic interview first
mcq.e: Worsening control, missed visits, fatigue and poor sleep after a major life change in a chronic-disease patient are classic cues of hidden depression. Depression worsens adherence and self-care, so screen first (Whooley/PHQ-2, then PHQ-9) before escalating diabetes treatment. Screening is a primary-care task and needs no psychiatric referral.
w: Wrong - escalating insulin ignores the likely driver of poor adherence; untreated depression will undermine any regimen.
Wrong - dietary advice is reasonable later, but it does not address the mood cues in his history.
Correct - chronic disease, fatigue, poor sleep and a major life change make him high-risk; brief screening then PHQ-9 is the right next step.
Wrong - organic screening has a place, but delaying the mood enquiry is unnecessary; the screening questions take one minute.
Wrong - depression screening and most mild-moderate depression are managed in primary care; routine referral is not the first step.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man with moderate depression refuses referral to the state psychiatric hospital because his neighbours would call him ‘gila’. He agrees to regular follow-up and treatment at his local Klinik Kesihatan.
Which rationale for integrating mental health into primary care does this best illustrate?
o: Local, familiar care reduces stigma and encourages early treatment
Primary care allows compulsory treatment without a court order
Primary care replaces the need for specialist psychiatric services
Primary care shifts the full cost of treatment onto the patient
Primary care guarantees specialist-level diagnosis at first contact
mcq.e: WHO/WONCA list reduced stigma, earlier help-seeking, accessibility, affordability, continuity and human-rights protection as reasons to integrate mental health into primary care. Being treated in a non-psychiatric, familiar clinic removes the label that keeps patients away. Specialist services remain essential for referral.
w: Correct - a familiar, non-psychiatric setting lowers stigma, so he accepts treatment early instead of avoiding care.
Wrong - compulsory treatment is governed by mental health legislation and is not a purpose of primary-care integration.
Wrong - integration complements specialist care; referral pathways remain for complex or high-risk cases.
Wrong - integration aims to make care more accessible and affordable, not to shift cost onto patients.
Wrong - primary care offers early identification and treatment of common disorders, not specialist-level diagnosis for all.

mcq.stem:
A 21-year-old student is seen at a Klinik Kesihatan late on a Friday, tearful after a relationship break-up. She has no suicidal thoughts, plan or self-harm, lives with supportive housemates and accepts a review on Monday, but asks who she can talk to over the weekend.
Which service is the most appropriate to give her?
o: Talian Kasih 15999, the JKM line for abuse and family crisis
One Stop Crisis Centre (OSCC) at the emergency department
The hospital Suspected Child Abuse and Neglect (SCAN) team
999 emergency ambulance if she feels sad again tonight
Talian HEAL 15555, the MOH psychosocial support line
mcq.e: Talian HEAL 15555 is the MOH psychosocial support line for emotional distress; Befrienders offers similar 24-hour support. Helplines supplement, never replace, a planned review and a safety assessment. OSCC, SCAN and Talian Kasih serve abuse and family crisis, and 999 is for emergencies.
w: Wrong - Talian Kasih (JKM) is mainly for abuse, domestic violence and family crises, not emotional support after a break-up.
Wrong - OSCC manages survivors of rape, domestic violence and abuse at the emergency department.
Wrong - the SCAN team handles suspected child abuse and neglect; she is an adult with no abuse.
Wrong - she is at low risk; an ambulance is for emergencies such as an imminent suicide attempt.
Correct - Talian HEAL gives MOH psychosocial support to distressed callers and fits a low-risk patient awaiting review.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old teacher reports 8 months of worrying most days about her job, money, her children’s health and her parents. She cannot switch the worry off, feels on edge, has neck and shoulder tension, poor sleep and snaps at her family. She has no discrete attacks of fear. TFT is normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Panic disorder
Generalised anxiety disorder
Social anxiety disorder
Adjustment disorder with anxiety
Illness anxiety disorder
mcq.e: Excessive, hard-to-control worry about many areas of life on more days than not for at least 6 months, with at least 3 of the 6 associated symptoms (here restlessness, muscle tension, sleep disturbance and irritability), is generalised anxiety disorder. Absence of discrete attacks argues against panic disorder. The worry is free-floating across domains rather than tied to one stressor, health or social scrutiny.
w: Wrong - panic disorder needs recurrent discrete attacks peaking within minutes; she has continuous worry instead.
Correct - multi-domain uncontrollable worry for over 6 months with 4 associated symptoms meets GAD criteria.
Wrong - social anxiety centres on fear of scrutiny in social situations, not general life worries.
Wrong - adjustment disorder follows an identifiable stressor and usually settles within 6 months; her worry is generalised.
Wrong - illness anxiety is preoccupation with having a serious illness; her worry spans work, money and family.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old man has worried excessively about work, his finances and his health for the past 3 months, more days than not. He finds it hard to control and reports restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration and muscle tension that affect his work. Examination and TFT are normal.
Which interpretation is correct?
o: Meets GAD criteria, as at least three associated symptoms are present
Falls short of GAD, as at least five associated symptoms are needed
Meets GAD criteria, as the worry occurs more days than not
Falls short of GAD, as worry must have lasted at least 6 months
Falls short of GAD, as the worry must focus on one single theme
mcq.e: DSM-5 GAD needs excessive, hard-to-control worry about several areas on more days than not for at least 6 months, plus at least 3 of 6 associated symptoms in adults. He has the symptoms but only 3 months of duration. He still deserves psychoeducation, lifestyle advice and review, and the diagnosis is reconsidered if symptoms persist.
w: Wrong - the symptom count is met, but the 6-month duration criterion is not.
Wrong - adults need 3 of the 6 associated symptoms, not 5.
Wrong - ‘more days than not’ is required but is not sufficient without 6 months of duration.
Correct - duration is the missing criterion; GAD requires worry on most days for at least 6 months.
Wrong - GAD worry spans several events or activities; a single focus suggests another disorder.

mcq.stem:
A 42-year-old woman completes the GAD-7 at a Klinik Kesihatan while waiting for her hypertension review. Her total score is 12.
How should this score be interpreted?
o: Minimal anxiety; no further assessment is needed
Mild anxiety; below the usual cut-off for probable GAD
Severe anxiety; urgent referral to psychiatry is required
Moderate anxiety; warrants a clinical assessment for GAD
Moderately severe anxiety; diagnostic of GAD on its own
mcq.e: GAD-7 bands are 0–4 minimal, 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate and 15–21 severe; a score of 10 or more is the usual cut-off for probable GAD. A screening score never makes the diagnosis by itself; it prompts a clinical assessment against DSM-5 criteria. ‘Moderately severe’ is a PHQ-9 band, not a GAD-7 band.
w: Wrong - minimal is 0–4; a score of 12 needs further assessment.
Wrong - mild is 5–9; 12 is above the cut-off of 10.
Wrong - severe is 15–21; a moderate score alone does not need urgent referral.
Correct - 12 lies in the moderate band (10–14) and is above the cut-off, so a clinical assessment for GAD follows.
Wrong - GAD-7 has no moderately severe band, and no screening score is diagnostic on its own.

mcq.stem:
During a BSSK health screening, a 40-year-old man scores 4 on the GAD-2 (feeling nervous or on edge; not being able to stop worrying). He has no suicidal thoughts and no medical history.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure him, as the GAD-2 is positive only at a score of 5 or more
Complete the full GAD-7 and a clinical assessment for anxiety
Start escitalopram 10 mg daily and review him in four weeks
Prescribe alprazolam 0.25 mg as needed for anxious periods
Refer him routinely to psychiatry to confirm the diagnosis
mcq.e: The GAD-2 is the first two items of the GAD-7, scored 0–6; a score of 3 or more is positive. A positive brief screen is followed by the full GAD-7 and a clinical assessment, not by treatment. Drug treatment or referral comes only after the diagnosis and severity are established.
w: Wrong - the GAD-2 cut-off is 3 or more, so a score of 4 is positive.
Correct - a positive GAD-2 is followed by the full GAD-7 and a clinical diagnostic assessment.
Wrong - starting an SSRI on a screening score alone skips diagnosis and severity assessment.
Wrong - benzodiazepines are second-line, short-term only, and never started on a screening result.
Wrong - anxiety disorders are assessed and usually managed in primary care; routine referral is not the next step.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old woman presents with 2 months of feeling anxious and restless, palpitations, a fine tremor and poor sleep. She has lost 4 kg despite a good appetite. Pulse is 108/min and regular, BP 128/70 mmHg. She drinks one cup of coffee a day.
Which investigation is most likely to reveal the cause?
o: Thyroid function test
12-lead ECG
Fasting plasma glucose
24-hour urine catecholamines
Full blood count
mcq.e: Anxiety with weight loss despite a good appetite, tremor and resting tachycardia points to hyperthyroidism, the classic medical mimic of an anxiety disorder. DSM-5 requires that anxiety is not attributable to a medical condition or substance, so TFT comes before labelling GAD. Phaeochromocytoma is far rarer and usually causes paroxysmal hypertension.
w: Correct - weight loss with a good appetite, tremor and tachycardia suggest thyrotoxicosis; TFT is the key test.
Wrong - an ECG is useful for palpitations, but a regular sinus tachycardia will not reveal the underlying cause.
Wrong - hypoglycaemia causes episodic symptoms, not persistent tachycardia with weight loss and good appetite.
Wrong - phaeochromocytoma is rare and usually paroxysmal with hypertension; her BP is normal.
Wrong - anaemia causes tachycardia and fatigue, but not tremor with weight loss despite good appetite.

mcq.stem:
A 10-year-old girl has worried most days for 7 months about exams, her parents’ safety and news events. Her mother says the worry is hard to stop and she has trouble falling asleep, but there is no restlessness, fatigue, irritability, muscle tension or poor concentration. Her grades are slipping.
Which interpretation is correct?
o: Does not meet GAD, as three associated symptoms are needed at any age
Does not meet GAD, as the diagnosis is not made before adolescence
Does not meet GAD, as worry must last at least 12 months in children
Meets GAD only if the GAD-7 score is 15 or more
Meets GAD, as children need only one associated symptom
mcq.e: DSM-5 GAD needs 3 of 6 associated symptoms in adults but only 1 in children. She has more than 6 months of multi-domain, hard-to-control worry, one associated symptom (sleep disturbance) and impairment, so she meets the criteria. Exclude medical causes and manage with child-focused CBT and parental involvement.
w: Wrong - the 3-symptom rule applies to adults; children need only one.
Wrong - GAD can be diagnosed in children; the criteria are simply modified.
Wrong - the duration is 6 months at all ages, not 12 months.
Wrong - GAD is diagnosed clinically; no GAD-7 threshold is required, and 15 marks severe anxiety.
Correct - with over 6 months of worry and one associated symptom, a child meets GAD criteria.

mcq.stem:
A 36-year-old woman with 9 months of excessive, uncontrollable worry has a GAD-7 of 11. Thyroid function is normal and she has no depression or suicidal thoughts. She wants to avoid medication because she is planning a pregnancy.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Alprazolam 0.25 mg twice daily for three months
Propranolol 40 mg twice daily as long-term therapy
Cognitive behavioural therapy with psychoeducation
Pregabalin 75 mg twice daily, titrated to response
Buspirone 5 mg three times daily as monotherapy
mcq.e: After psychoeducation and lifestyle measures, CBT is the first-line psychological treatment for GAD and is the obvious choice for a patient who wants to avoid drugs. An SSRI is the first-line drug only if medication is required. Benzodiazepines are second-line and short-term only; pregabalin is reserved for when SSRIs/SNRIs are unsuitable.
w: Wrong - benzodiazepines are second-line, limited to 2–4 weeks, and three months risks dependence.
Wrong - beta-blockers ease palpitations and tremor but do not treat the worry of GAD.
Correct - CBT with psychoeducation is first-line psychological therapy and respects her wish to avoid medication.
Wrong - pregabalin is an option only when SSRIs and SNRIs are unsuitable, and she prefers no drugs.
Wrong - buspirone is a drug she wishes to avoid and is not first-line; it is slow in onset.

mcq.stem:
An 8-year-old boy has had abdominal pain and nausea on school mornings for 6 weeks, settling by midday at home and absent at weekends. Since his father was hospitalised, he follows his mother around the house, will not sleep alone and has nightmares that she will die. Examination is normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Specific phobia, situational type
Separation anxiety disorder
Generalised anxiety disorder
Selective mutism
Social anxiety disorder
mcq.e: Developmentally inappropriate fear of harm to, or separation from, an attachment figure with nightmares, refusal to sleep alone and somatic complaints on school mornings is separation anxiety disorder. In children the duration needed is at least 4 weeks. School refusal here is driven by leaving mother, not by school itself.
w: Wrong - a situational phobia is fear of the situation itself; his fear is about losing his mother.
Correct - fear of separation, nightmares about the mother dying, clinging and school-morning symptoms over 4 weeks fit.
Wrong - GAD is multi-domain worry; his worry centres on separation from one attachment figure.
Wrong - selective mutism is failure to speak in specific settings despite speaking elsewhere.
Wrong - social anxiety is fear of scrutiny by peers or others, not of separation from a parent.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old woman reports that for the past 2 months, whenever her husband travels for work, she becomes intensely afraid he will be killed or leave her. She phones him up to 20 times a day and cannot sleep alone. There is no history of panic attacks.
Which interpretation is correct?
o: Meets criteria for separation anxiety disorder, as 4 weeks have passed
Cannot be separation anxiety disorder, as it occurs only in childhood
Meets criteria only if she also had separation anxiety as a child
Cannot be diagnosed unless she has had a childhood traumatic event
Does not yet meet the duration, as adults typically need 6 months
mcq.e: Separation anxiety disorder can occur in adults, with partners as attachment figures. The duration threshold is at least 4 weeks in children and adolescents but typically 6 months or more in adults. Childhood adversity is a risk factor, not a requirement.
w: Wrong - 4 weeks is the threshold for children and adolescents, not adults.
Wrong - DSM-5 recognises adult separation anxiety disorder; partners can be attachment figures.
Wrong - childhood separation anxiety is not required for an adult diagnosis.
Wrong - childhood trauma raises risk but is not a diagnostic criterion.
Correct - adults typically need 6 months of symptoms, so 2 months falls short; review and support her meanwhile.

mcq.stem:
A 7-year-old girl with 3 months of excessive distress on separation from her mother now refuses to go to school. Physical examination is normal and she has no other psychiatric symptoms. Her mother asks whether she should keep her at home until the fear settles.
What is the most appropriate first-line management?
o: A medical letter excusing her from school until the fear has settled
Start fluoxetine 10 mg daily and review after six weeks
CBT with gradual exposure, involving parents and the school
Home-schooling with her mother for the rest of the school year
Low-dose diazepam each school morning for two to four weeks
mcq.e: Separation anxiety disorder is managed with psychoeducation for child and parents, then CBT with gradual exposure to separation, family involvement and school collaboration. Avoidance (staying home) maintains the fear, so an early return to school is a goal. An SSRI is considered only for moderate–severe or persistent cases, usually with CBT.
w: Wrong - excusing her from school reinforces avoidance and keeps the anxiety going.
Wrong - an SSRI is considered only for moderate–severe or persistent symptoms, not as first-line.
Correct - CBT with graded exposure, parental involvement and school collaboration is first-line.
Wrong - home-schooling with the attachment figure maximises avoidance and worsens the disorder.
Wrong - benzodiazepines have no first-line role in childhood anxiety and risk dependence.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old university student avoids tutorials, eats alone and skips oral presentations. He fears others will notice him blushing and trembling and think he is stupid. When he must speak, he sweats, his mouth goes dry and he stumbles over words. This has lasted a year and he is failing two modules.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Social anxiety disorder
Agoraphobia
Panic disorder
Generalised anxiety disorder
Avoidant personality disorder
mcq.e: Persistent fear of being watched and negatively judged in social situations, with avoidance, physical symptoms, over 6 months and functional impairment, is social anxiety disorder. Ask what the patient fears will happen: humiliation (social anxiety) vs being trapped (agoraphobia) vs the attack itself (panic). Avoidant personality disorder is a pervasive lifelong personality pattern, not a focused fear.
w: Correct - fear of scrutiny and embarrassment with avoidance, autonomic symptoms and impairment for a year fits.
Wrong - agoraphobia is fear of being unable to escape or get help, not of being judged.
Wrong - his symptoms arise only in feared social situations, not as unexpected attacks.
Wrong - GAD is multi-domain worry; his fear is specific to social evaluation.
Wrong - avoidant personality disorder is a pervasive personality pattern; a focused social fear is the better fit.

mcq.stem:
A 15-year-old girl is brought by her mother, who says she is ‘too quiet’. She is hesitant in new groups but joins school activities after a few minutes, has two close friends, does well academically and denies distress or avoidance.
What is the most appropriate interpretation?
o: Social anxiety disorder needing a course of CBT
Selective mutism needing a speech-language referral
Avoidant personality disorder needing psychiatric review
Normal shy temperament; no anxiety disorder present
Autism spectrum disorder needing developmental assessment
mcq.e: Shyness is a temperament: the person feels uneasy at first but still participates, without major distress or impairment. Social anxiety disorder needs intense fear, avoidance, at least 6 months and functional impairment. Labelling normal shyness risks unnecessary treatment.
w: Wrong - she has no avoidance, distress or impairment, so social anxiety disorder is not present.
Wrong - selective mutism is consistent failure to speak where speech is expected; she speaks and participates.
Wrong - personality disorders are not diagnosed on mild shyness, and she has no pervasive avoidance.
Correct - warming up, friendships and good function without distress describe normal shyness.
Wrong - she has normal social reciprocity and friendships, with no features suggesting autism.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old lecturer has trembling hands, a pounding heart and a shaky voice only when giving conference talks a few times a year. He is comfortable in all other social situations. He has no asthma, and his pulse is 72/min.
Which treatment is most appropriate before his talks?
o: Propranolol 10–40 mg about one hour before the talk
Sertraline 50 mg daily, continued for twelve months
Alprazolam 0.5 mg three times daily for one month
Buspirone 10 mg on the morning of each talk
Pregabalin 150 mg daily, continued long term
mcq.e: Fear limited to speaking or performing in public is the ‘performance only’ specifier of social anxiety disorder. Occasional, predictable events are well served by situational propranolol, which blocks tremor and palpitations; check for asthma and bradycardia first. Daily SSRIs and CBT are for generalised social anxiety.
w: Correct - situational propranolol suits infrequent performance-only anxiety in a patient without asthma.
Wrong - a year of daily SSRI is excessive for a few talks a year without generalised social anxiety.
Wrong - regular benzodiazepines risk sedation and dependence and impair performance.
Wrong - buspirone takes 2–4 weeks to work and is useless as a single pre-event dose.
Wrong - long-term pregabalin is not indicated for occasional performance anxiety.

mcq.stem:
A 5-year-old girl has not spoken a word at kindergarten for 4 months, although she chats fluently with her family at home in the same language used at school. She makes good eye contact, plays imaginatively and her hearing test is normal. Teachers say she clings to her mother at drop-off.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Autism spectrum disorder
Developmental language disorder
Selective mutism
Normal shyness
Intellectual disability
mcq.e: Consistent failure to speak in a setting where speech is expected, despite normal speech elsewhere, for at least 1 month and interfering with education or social communication, is selective mutism. Exclude lack of fluency in the school language, communication disorders and autism, all of which are absent here. Clinging, shyness and fear of embarrassment are associated features.
w: Wrong - she has good eye contact, imaginative play and fluent speech at home, which argue against autism.
Wrong - her language is fluent at home, so the problem is situational, not a language deficit.
Correct - 4 months of silence at kindergarten with fluent speech at home in the same language fits.
Wrong - shy children still speak once settled; 4 months of total silence with impairment is beyond shyness.
Wrong - her fluent speech and imaginative play make global intellectual impairment unlikely.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old boy started Year 1 three weeks ago. His teacher reports he has not spoken in class, though he whispers to one classmate. At home he talks normally and is cheerful. Development, hearing and language are normal.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Diagnose selective mutism and refer to child psychiatry now
Start fluoxetine 5 mg daily to reduce the anticipatory anxiety
Refer urgently for speech-language therapy and audiometry
Explain this is common when settling in and review in a month
Advise the school to require him to speak before he can play
mcq.e: Selective mutism needs at least 1 month of failure to speak and explicitly excludes the first month of school, when silence while settling in is common. Watchful waiting with reassurance and gentle encouragement is appropriate. Pressuring the child to speak increases anxiety.
w: Wrong - the first month of school is excluded, so the diagnosis cannot yet be made.
Wrong - an SSRI is only for severe or refractory selective mutism, never as a first step.
Wrong - development, hearing and language are normal; urgent referral is not indicated.
Correct - silence in the first weeks of school is common; reassure and review after the first month.
Wrong - coercion increases anxiety; behavioural approaches use gradual exposure and positive reinforcement.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old woman has had six sudden episodes over 2 months of pounding heart, chest tightness, tingling fingers and a feeling she is about to die. Each peaks within 5 minutes and settles within 20 minutes, sometimes waking her from sleep. She now worries constantly about the next one and has stopped jogging. ECG, TFT and glucose are normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Generalised anxiety disorder
Agoraphobia
Supraventricular tachycardia
Hyperthyroidism
Panic disorder
mcq.e: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks peaking within minutes, followed by at least 1 month of worry about further attacks and behaviour change (avoiding exercise), define panic disorder. Nocturnal attacks are common. Normal ECG, TFT and glucose make the main medical mimics unlikely.
w: Wrong - GAD is continuous multi-domain worry, not discrete attacks peaking within minutes.
Wrong - agoraphobia is avoidance of places where escape is hard; she avoids exertion, not places.
Wrong - SVT is possible, but the fear of dying, tingling and normal ECG with this pattern favour panic disorder.
Wrong - a normal TFT excludes hyperthyroidism.
Correct - recurrent unexpected attacks with over a month of anticipatory worry and avoidance of exercise fit.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old man is brought into the Klinik Kesihatan treatment room breathing rapidly and terrified, with tingling around his mouth and cramping of his hands. Pulse 110/min, SpO2 99% on air, capillary glucose 5.6 mmol/L, and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia only. He has had similar episodes before.
What is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Have him rebreathe into a paper bag until the tingling settles
Reassure him in a calm room and coach slow, steady breathing
Give intravenous calcium gluconate for the carpopedal spasm
Give intramuscular diazepam 10 mg and observe for one hour
Give nebulised salbutamol for presumed acute bronchospasm
mcq.e: Acute panic is managed with reassurance, a calm environment and controlled slow breathing, after excluding important medical causes as done here. Paper-bag rebreathing is avoided because it can cause hypoxia if the cause is actually cardiac or respiratory. The carpopedal spasm reflects alkalosis-induced low ionised calcium and settles with normal breathing.
w: Wrong - paper-bag rebreathing risks hypoxia and is no longer recommended.
Correct - reassurance, a calm setting and slow controlled breathing are first-line for an acute panic attack.
Wrong - total calcium is normal; tetany results from respiratory alkalosis and resolves as breathing slows.
Wrong - parenteral benzodiazepines are unnecessary for a typical panic attack and add sedation risk.
Wrong - he has no wheeze or hypoxia, and salbutamol would worsen tachycardia and tremor.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 3 weeks of sudden episodes of sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger and a sense of dread. They occur late in the morning when she delays lunch and settle within 15 minutes after she eats. Her gliclazide was increased to 160 mg twice daily last month; HbA1c is 6.2%. Examination and ECG between episodes are normal.
What is the most likely cause of her episodes?
o: Hypoglycaemia due to gliclazide
Recurrent unexpected panic attacks
Generalised anxiety disorder
Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
Subclinical hyperthyroidism
mcq.e: Adrenergic symptoms that cluster before meals, follow a sulphonylurea dose increase and resolve with food point to hypoglycaemia, a classic panic mimic. The slides stress excluding important medical causes before labelling panic. Confirm with a capillary glucose during an episode and reduce the gliclazide dose.
w: Correct - timing before meals, relief with food, a recent dose increase and a tight HbA1c make sulphonylurea hypoglycaemia the cause until proven otherwise.
Wrong - panic attacks are unexpected and not tied to fasting or relieved by eating; an organic mimic must be excluded first.
Wrong - GAD causes persistent free-floating worry over at least 6 months, not discrete pre-meal attacks.
Wrong - paroxysmal AF causes palpitations but not hunger, and would not settle reliably with food.
Wrong - hyperthyroidism gives continuous symptoms with weight loss and tachycardia, not episodes linked to meals.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old man has had recurrent unexpected attacks of chest tightness, palpitations, tingling and fear of dying for 4 months. Between attacks he worries constantly about the next one and has stopped driving. ECG, TFT and glucose are normal. A friend gave him alprazolam, which helps, and he asks for a regular supply.
What is the most appropriate long-term pharmacological plan?
o: Regular alprazolam 0.5 mg three times daily for 6 months
Propranolol 40 mg twice daily as maintenance therapy
Amitriptyline 75 mg at night as the first-choice drug
Sertraline started at a low dose and titrated, with CBT
Pregabalin 150 mg twice daily as the first-choice drug
mcq.e: Recurrent unexpected attacks with a month or more of anticipatory worry and avoidance is panic disorder. An SSRI is first-line drug treatment, started low because early activation can worsen panic, and combined with CBT. Long-term benzodiazepines are specifically to be avoided because of tolerance, dependence and withdrawal.
w: Wrong - the slides say avoid long-term benzodiazepines; regular alprazolam for months risks dependence and rebound panic.
Wrong - beta-blockers blunt palpitations only and do not prevent panic attacks or the anticipatory worry.
Wrong - tricyclics work but are not first choice because of side-effects and danger in overdose.
Correct - an SSRI started low and titrated, plus CBT, is first-line long-term treatment for panic disorder.
Wrong - pregabalin has a role in GAD when SSRIs/SNRIs are unsuitable; it is not first choice for panic disorder.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old woman with recurrent panic attacks has started CBT at a hospital psychology clinic. In the session the therapist asks her to spin on a chair and breathe rapidly through a narrow straw to bring on dizziness and breathlessness, then to stay with the sensations without escaping until they settle.
Which technique is being used?
o: Systematic desensitisation
Interoceptive exposure
Flooding to an external cue
Cognitive restructuring
Biofeedback training
mcq.e: Interoceptive exposure deliberately provokes the feared bodily sensations of panic so the patient learns they are harmless and fade on their own. It targets the catastrophic misinterpretation at the core of the cognitive model of panic. It differs from exposure to external situations, which is used for phobic avoidance.
w: Wrong - systematic desensitisation pairs relaxation with a graded hierarchy of external feared situations.
Correct - inducing dizziness and breathlessness on purpose and staying with them is interoceptive exposure.
Wrong - flooding is prolonged maximal exposure to an external feared object or situation, not to body sensations.
Wrong - cognitive restructuring challenges catastrophic thoughts verbally; it does not provoke symptoms.
Wrong - biofeedback uses monitored signals such as heart rate to train relaxation, not symptom provocation.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old clerk with recurrent unexpected panic attacks has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for 12 weeks and attended six CBT sessions. She is adherent but still has two attacks a week. On closer questioning she drinks four or five cans of beer most nights to calm herself and feels shaky most mornings.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Add clonazepam 0.5 mg twice daily for long-term control
Switch sertraline to fluoxetine at once without tapering
Add propranolol 40 mg three times daily for her symptoms
Increase sertraline to 200 mg daily in a single step
Reassess the diagnosis and address the alcohol use first
mcq.e: When panic symptoms persist despite adequate treatment, the slides advise reassessing the diagnosis and looking for comorbidity before escalating drugs. Nightly drinking with morning shakiness suggests alcohol dependence and withdrawal, which both mimic and drive panic. Refer if still refractory after this is addressed.
w: Wrong - adding a benzodiazepine to someone drinking heavily risks dependence and dangerous sedation; long-term use is to be avoided.
Wrong - switching SSRIs ignores the comorbidity that explains non-response.
Wrong - a beta-blocker treats palpitations only and does nothing for alcohol-driven symptoms.
Wrong - escalating the dose before addressing comorbid alcohol use is unlikely to help.
Correct - persistent symptoms call for reassessment of diagnosis and comorbidity; alcohol use and withdrawal must be tackled.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old engineer attends a Klinik Kesihatan because his company wants him to fly to Sabah monthly. For 2 years he has refused all flights; even booking a ticket brings on palpitations, sweating and trembling. He is comfortable in shopping malls, crowds, buses and when driving alone, has no unexpected attacks and does not worry about others judging him.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Agoraphobia with panic attacks
Panic disorder with avoidance
Specific phobia, situational type
Social anxiety, performance-only
Generalised anxiety disorder
mcq.e: Fear confined to one situation (flying), with marked avoidance and impairment for more than 6 months, is a specific phobia of the situational type. Agoraphobia needs fear in at least two of the five DSM-5 situation groups, and he is comfortable in crowds and on buses. The absence of unexpected attacks argues against panic disorder.
w: Wrong - agoraphobia requires fear of at least 2 situation groups; he copes with crowds, buses and malls.
Wrong - panic disorder needs recurrent unexpected attacks; his anxiety is cued by one situation only.
Correct - fear and avoidance limited to flying, lasting over 6 months with impairment, is a situational specific phobia.
Wrong - social anxiety centres on fear of scrutiny or embarrassment, which he denies.
Wrong - GAD is diffuse worry about many things, not fear focused on a single situation.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old woman is brought by her daughter to a Klinik Kesihatan. For 8 months she has avoided the pasar malam, LRT trains, queues at the bank and open car parks, and will not leave the house unless her daughter goes with her. She fears she would collapse and be unable to get out or get help. She is not worried about embarrassment and has no fear of being apart from her daughter at home.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Agoraphobia
Social anxiety disorder
Specific phobia, situational type
Generalised anxiety disorder
Separation anxiety disorder
mcq.e: Fear and avoidance of several situation groups (public transport, open spaces, queues/crowds, being outside the home alone) because escape or help might be unavailable, lasting 6 months or more, is agoraphobia. DSM-5 needs at least 2 of the 5 groups. Note: the slide calls agoraphobia a subtype of panic disorder; since DSM-5 it is a separate diagnosis that may coexist with panic disorder.
w: Correct - fear across 4 situation groups because escape or help may be unavailable, for 8 months, is agoraphobia.
Wrong - social anxiety is fear of scrutiny and embarrassment, which she denies.
Wrong - specific phobia is limited to one object or situation, not multiple situation groups.
Wrong - GAD is chronic diffuse worry, not situational fear with avoidance.
Wrong - she needs a companion because of fear of being trapped, not distress at separation from an attachment figure.

mcq.stem:
A 19-year-old student faints while blood is taken for a pre-employment check at a Klinik Kesihatan. She has fainted at injections since childhood and avoids dental treatment. After the needle her pulse fell from 110 to 48/min and BP to 85/50 mmHg before she recovered fully lying flat. She still needs the blood test.
What is the best approach for the next venepuncture?
o: Give oral diazepam 5 mg one hour before
Give propranolol 40 mg before the procedure
Sit her upright and distract her by talking
Take blood lying down and teach applied tension
Postpone all blood tests until CBT is complete
mcq.e: Blood-injection-injury phobia is unique among phobias because the initial surge in heart rate is followed by a vasovagal drop in pulse and blood pressure, causing fainting. Lying the patient down and teaching applied tension (tensing large muscles to raise BP) prevents syncope. Drugs that lower pulse or BP make it worse.
w: Wrong - sedation does not prevent the vasovagal drop and adds risk; it is not the recommended approach.
Wrong - propranolol would deepen the bradycardia and hypotension that cause her to faint.
Wrong - sitting upright makes vasovagal syncope more likely; distraction alone is insufficient.
Correct - a supine position plus applied tension counters the biphasic vasovagal response.
Wrong - delaying a needed test is unnecessary when simple measures allow it to be done safely.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old postman was bitten by a dog at age 9. For years he has crossed roads to avoid dogs; now he refuses routes with dogs and has received a warning at work. When he sees a dog he trembles, sweats and has a racing heart. He has no other anxiety symptoms and his mood is normal.
What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
o: Daily sertraline for six months
Exposure-based CBT with graded steps
Diazepam 5 mg before each delivery round
Propranolol 40 mg before each delivery round
Supportive counselling and reassurance alone
mcq.e: Specific phobia responds well to CBT with gradual (graded) exposure, which is first-line and has durable benefit. Drugs have little role: benzodiazepines can block the learning that exposure depends on and cause dependence. Reassurance without exposure leaves avoidance in place.
w: Wrong - SSRIs are not first-line for an isolated specific phobia.
Correct - graded exposure within CBT (desensitisation) is the treatment of choice for specific phobia.
Wrong - regular benzodiazepines cause dependence and undermine exposure learning.
Wrong - a beta-blocker blunts tremor and palpitations but does not treat the fear or avoidance.
Wrong - reassurance alone does not extinguish the conditioned fear; exposure is needed.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man with a lifelong fear of cockroaches agrees, after full explanation and consent, to a therapy in which he is placed directly in a room with many cockroaches. No relaxation training or step-by-step hierarchy is used, and he stays until his anxiety falls on its own.
Which behavioural technique is this?
o: Systematic desensitisation
Progressive muscle relaxation
Cognitive restructuring
Graded virtual-reality exposure
Flooding
mcq.e: Flooding is immediate, prolonged exposure to the most feared stimulus until anxiety extinguishes, without a hierarchy. Systematic desensitisation instead pairs relaxation with gradual steps up a fear hierarchy. Both are behavioural techniques listed on the slides; flooding is faster but more distressing and needs consent.
w: Wrong - systematic desensitisation uses relaxation and a graded hierarchy, both absent here.
Wrong - progressive muscle relaxation is a relaxation skill, not an exposure method.
Wrong - cognitive restructuring challenges thoughts rather than exposing him to the stimulus.
Wrong - graded virtual-reality exposure is stepwise and simulated, not immediate real exposure.
Correct - immediate, prolonged exposure to the most feared stimulus without a hierarchy is flooding.

mcq.stem:
A 31-year-old teacher reports that for 3 months she has avoided crowded shopping malls, buses and standing in queues, and goes out only with her husband, because she fears she could not escape or get help if she felt faint. Examination, FBC and TFT are normal. She asks whether she has a definite diagnosis.
What is the minimum duration of fear or avoidance usually required by DSM-5 before this diagnosis is confirmed?
o: 2 weeks
1 month
6 months
3 months
12 months
mcq.e: Her fear of several situations where escape or help may be unavailable fits agoraphobia, which requires persistent fear, anxiety or avoidance typically lasting 6 months or more. The 1-month figure belongs to panic disorder (worry or behaviour change after an attack). Until 6 months, offer support and review rather than a firm label.
w: Wrong - 2 weeks is the duration for a major depressive episode.
Wrong - 1 month applies to the worry or behaviour change after a panic attack in panic disorder.
Correct - agoraphobia (like specific phobia) typically requires 6 months or more of fear or avoidance.
Wrong - 3 months is not a DSM-5 threshold for agoraphobia; she is still short of the required duration.
Wrong - 12 months is longer than DSM-5 requires.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old violinist with asthma, using a budesonide-formoterol inhaler, attends a Klinik Kesihatan. She has severe tremor and pounding palpitations before every audition but is otherwise well, with no anxiety between performances. She asks for a tablet to take before her next audition.
Which medication is contraindicated for her?
o: Escitalopram 5 mg daily
Sertraline 25 mg daily
Propranolol 20 mg before playing
Buspirone 5 mg twice daily long term
Venlafaxine 37.5 mg daily
mcq.e: Beta-blockers such as propranolol relieve the physical symptoms of performance anxiety (tremor, palpitations) and are often used for this purpose. However, non-selective beta-blockers can cause severe bronchospasm and are contraindicated in asthma. Offer CBT-based approaches instead, and remember the other options are not contraindicated even if they are not ideal for purely situational symptoms.
w: Wrong - escitalopram is not first choice for isolated performance symptoms, but asthma does not contraindicate it.
Wrong - sertraline is safe in asthma; it is simply not needed for purely situational symptoms.
Correct - non-selective beta-blockade can trigger life-threatening bronchospasm in asthma.
Wrong - buspirone is a slow-onset drug for chronic anxiety; it is not contraindicated in asthma.
Wrong - venlafaxine is unnecessary here but carries no asthma contraindication.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old woman has had 9 months of excessive, hard-to-control worry about her family, finances and work, with restlessness, muscle tension, poor sleep and irritability. GAD-7 is 15 and she has no suicidal thoughts. A neighbour lent her alprazolam, which ‘works wonders’, and she asks for a regular prescription.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Regular alprazolam 0.5 mg three times daily as her maintenance drug
Clonazepam 0.5 mg at night for at least 6 months, then review
Propranolol 40 mg twice daily as her sole long-term treatment
Buspirone alone, avoiding SSRIs because of their side-effects
Escitalopram with CBT; any benzodiazepine for 2–4 weeks only
mcq.e: SSRIs or SNRIs plus CBT are first-line for generalised anxiety. Benzodiazepines are second-line and short-term only (2–4 weeks) because of sedation, tolerance, dependence and withdrawal. Maintenance benzodiazepines are the classic trap.
w: Wrong - regular alprazolam as maintenance leads to tolerance and dependence; benzodiazepines are short-term only.
Wrong - six months of clonazepam is long-term benzodiazepine use, which the slides warn against.
Wrong - beta-blockers ease physical symptoms only and do not treat the worry.
Wrong - buspirone is an option for chronic anxiety but is not first-line; SSRIs should not be avoided without reason.
Correct - an SSRI with CBT is first-line; a benzodiazepine, if used at all, is limited to 2–4 weeks.

mcq.stem:
A 33-year-old man with 8 months of excessive worry, poor sleep and muscle tension starts escitalopram 5 mg daily at a Klinik Kesihatan. He has no suicidal thoughts and no medical illness. He asks how often he needs to come back.
Which follow-up schedule is most appropriate?
o: At 1–2 weeks, then every 2–4 weeks for 3 months, then 3-monthly
At 4 weeks, then every 4 weeks for 6 months, then 6-monthly
At 6 weeks, then every 3 months for the first year of treatment
At 3 months, then yearly while he stays on the medication
Only if side-effects occur or his symptoms clearly get worse
mcq.e: The slides advise monitoring medication initially at 1–2 weeks, then every 2–4 weeks for the first 3 months, and 3-monthly after that. The early visit catches side-effects, early activation and non-adherence, which are commonest in the first weeks. Waiting a month or more misses this window.
w: Correct - early review at 1–2 weeks, then 2–4 weekly for 3 months, then 3-monthly matches the recommended schedule.
Wrong - a first review at 4 weeks misses early side-effects and activation.
Wrong - 6 weeks is far too late for the first review of a new SSRI.
Wrong - a first review at 3 months leaves him unsupported through the riskiest period.
Wrong - passive follow-up misses non-adherence, side-effects and emerging risk.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old woman started sertraline 25 mg daily 6 days ago for recurrent panic attacks. She returns to the Klinik Kesihatan feeling more jittery and restless, with mild nausea and slightly worse anxiety. She denies suicidal thoughts and has no fever, tremor or clonus.
What is the most appropriate response?
o: Stop sertraline today and switch her to venlafaxine
Add alprazolam 0.5 mg three times daily long term
Double the sertraline dose to speed up the response
Explain early effects usually settle; continue and review
Stop sertraline as she is clearly intolerant of SSRIs
mcq.e: Jitteriness, nausea and a transient rise in anxiety are common in the first 1–2 weeks of an SSRI and usually settle; this is why SSRIs are started low in panic disorder. Counselling beforehand and a supportive early review improve adherence. Check for suicidality, especially in young people, and look for features of serotonin syndrome.
w: Wrong - early activation is expected and transient; switching now loses a likely effective drug.
Wrong - long-term benzodiazepine use is to be avoided; a short course is rarely needed for early activation.
Wrong - increasing the dose would worsen the activation symptoms.
Correct - reassure that early side-effects usually ease within 1–2 weeks, continue the low dose and review soon.
Wrong - mild early activation does not mean intolerance of the whole class.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man has had 2 years of excessive worry with tension, poor sleep and irritability. Sertraline and later escitalopram both caused hyponatraemia (Na 126 mmol/L), and venlafaxine raised his BP to 168/100 mmHg. He is now on CBT but remains impaired. The psychiatrist judges SSRIs and SNRIs unsuitable.
Which drug is the most appropriate option?
o: Clonazepam 0.5 mg twice daily long term
Pregabalin, titrated, alongside CBT
Haloperidol 1.5 mg at night
Propranolol 40 mg three times daily
Fluoxetine 20 mg once daily
mcq.e: The slides list pregabalin as an option for generalised anxiety when SSRIs and SNRIs are unsuitable. Counsel about dizziness, sedation and its misuse potential, and reduce the dose in renal impairment. Long-term benzodiazepines and antipsychotics are not appropriate maintenance treatments.
w: Wrong - long-term benzodiazepines cause tolerance, dependence and withdrawal.
Correct - pregabalin is the recommended alternative for GAD when SSRIs/SNRIs cannot be used.
Wrong - antipsychotics are not used for uncomplicated anxiety and carry significant side-effects.
Wrong - propranolol treats physical symptoms only, not chronic worry.
Wrong - fluoxetine is another SSRI and risks the same hyponatraemia.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old woman on sertraline 100 mg daily for anxiety was given tramadol at a private clinic for knee pain 2 days ago. She now presents agitated and sweating, with diarrhoea and tremor. T 38.4 °C, HR 118/min, pupils dilated, reflexes brisk with inducible ankle clonus. She takes no other drugs and drinks no alcohol.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome
Thyroid storm
Anticholinergic toxicity
Alcohol withdrawal syndrome
mcq.e: An SSRI combined with tramadol (a serotonergic opioid) followed within days by agitation, autonomic instability and neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia) is serotonin syndrome. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops more slowly, with lead-pipe rigidity and reduced reflexes. Stop the serotonergic drugs and refer urgently.
w: Wrong - NMS follows antipsychotics, develops over days with rigidity and slowed reflexes, not clonus.
Correct - SSRI plus tramadol with clonus, hyperthermia and autonomic features is serotonin syndrome.
Wrong - thyroid storm does not cause inducible clonus and has no link to the new drug.
Wrong - anticholinergic toxicity gives dry, hot skin and urinary retention, not sweating and diarrhoea.
Wrong - she does not drink, and withdrawal does not explain the drug-timed onset with clonus.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old man with generalised anxiety has been managed at a Klinik Kesihatan for 7 months. He took sertraline 150 mg for 10 weeks, then venlafaxine 150 mg for 12 weeks, both adherently, plus eight CBT sessions. GAD-7 is still 17, he has been on sick leave for 2 months, and he denies suicidal thoughts or substance use.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer to psychiatry for specialist assessment
Add regular alprazolam and continue in the KK
Switch to a third SSRI and review in 3 months
Stop all drugs and continue relaxation alone
Add propranolol and continue current care
mcq.e: Failure of at least two adequate treatments (correct dose and duration) with severe functional impairment is a referral criterion for anxiety disorders. Other triggers include suicide risk, diagnostic uncertainty and comorbid psychosis, bipolar disorder or substance misuse. Adding long-term benzodiazepines in primary care is not the answer to treatment resistance.
w: Correct - two failed adequate treatments plus marked impairment warrant specialist review.
Wrong - long-term benzodiazepines are to be avoided and do not address treatment resistance.
Wrong - repeating trials in primary care delays specialist care after two adequate failures.
Wrong - stopping effective-class drugs without a plan risks relapse and discontinuation symptoms.
Wrong - propranolol only blunts physical symptoms and does not address resistant illness.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old woman attends a Klinik Kesihatan for blood pressure review. When asked the two Whooley questions about the past month, she answers ‘no’ to feeling down, depressed or hopeless but ‘yes’ to having little interest or pleasure in doing things.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure her, as screening is negative without low mood
Repeat both questions at her next visit in 3 months
Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily and review in 4 weeks
Refer her to psychiatry for a formal interview
Complete a PHQ-9 and a clinical assessment today
mcq.e: The Whooley screen is positive if the answer to either question is yes. A positive screen calls for a fuller assessment the same day (PHQ-9 and clinical interview against diagnostic criteria). Anhedonia alone is a core symptom of depression, so absence of low mood does not make the screen negative.
w: Wrong - one ‘yes’ answer is a positive screen; anhedonia is a core symptom of depression.
Wrong - delaying assessment of a positive screen for 3 months risks missing depression and suicide risk.
Wrong - treatment should not start before the diagnosis and severity are established.
Wrong - screening and assessment are primary-care tasks; routine referral is not the next step.
Correct - a positive Whooley screen leads to PHQ-9 and clinical assessment now.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old lorry driver completes a PHQ-9 at a Klinik Kesihatan after a positive two-question screen. His total score is 16, and he scores 0 on the final item about thoughts of death or self-harm.
Which interpretation of this score is correct?
o: Mild symptoms; watchful waiting and repeat PHQ-9
Severe symptoms; he needs urgent hospital admission
Minimal symptoms; the screen is effectively negative
Moderately severe; above the usual cut-off of 10
Moderate symptoms; below the cut-off for probable MDD
mcq.e: PHQ-9 bands are 0–4 minimal, 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–19 moderately severe and 20–27 severe; 10 or more is the usual cut-off for probable MDD. A score of 16 is moderately severe and warrants active treatment after confirming the diagnosis clinically. The score supports, but never replaces, the clinical interview.
w: Wrong - mild is 5–9; 16 is well above that band.
Wrong - severe starts at 20, and admission depends on risk and psychosis rather than the score alone.
Wrong - minimal is 0–4.
Correct - 15–19 is moderately severe, and 16 is above the usual cut-off of 10.
Wrong - moderate is 10–14, and any score of 10 or more is at or above the cut-off.

mcq.stem:
A 23-year-old university student completes a PHQ-9 at a Klinik Kesihatan. Her total is 8. On item 9, thoughts that she would be better off dead or of hurting herself, she has ticked ‘several days’. She is quiet and makes little eye contact.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure her, as the total is below the cut-off of 10
Repeat the PHQ-9 in 2 weeks before deciding further
Ask directly about suicidal ideas, plans and intent now
Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review in 4 weeks
Send a routine referral letter to the psychiatry clinic
mcq.e: Any positive score on PHQ-9 item 9 requires a direct suicide risk assessment at the same visit, whatever the total score. Ask about ideas, plans, intent, means, past attempts and protective factors, then act on the level of risk. A low total does not exclude risk.
w: Wrong - a low total never cancels out a positive item 9.
Wrong - waiting 2 weeks could miss an imminent risk.
Correct - a positive item 9 demands a direct suicide risk assessment today.
Wrong - starting treatment before assessing risk is unsafe; risk assessment comes first.
Wrong - a routine letter does not address possible immediate risk; assess first, then refer urgently if needed.

mcq.stem:
A 41-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan with 3 weeks of insomnia nearly every night, fatigue, poor concentration at work, 4 kg unintentional weight loss and excessive guilt over a small mistake at work. He denies feeling sad and still enjoys futsal and time with his children most days. There is no medical illness or substance use.
Which additional finding is required before DSM-5 major depressive disorder can be diagnosed?
o: Symptoms persisting for at least 1 month
A sixth symptom from the list of nine
Recurrent thoughts of death or of suicide
Depressed mood or loss of interest most days
Psychomotor slowing observed by others
mcq.e: DSM-5 criterion A needs at least 5 of 9 symptoms over the same 2-week period, and at least one must be depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure. He already has five symptoms for 3 weeks, but neither core symptom, so the criteria are not met however many other symptoms are added. Look for another cause of his symptoms and review.
w: Wrong - the DSM-5 duration is 2 weeks, which he already exceeds.
Wrong - adding a sixth symptom does not help if neither core symptom is present.
Wrong - suicidal thoughts are one of the nine symptoms but cannot substitute for a core symptom.
Correct - at least one of the five symptoms must be depressed mood or loss of interest/pleasure.
Wrong - psychomotor change is another non-core symptom and does not satisfy the core requirement.

mcq.stem:
A 15-year-old boy is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan by his mother. For 4 weeks he has been irritable and snapping at the family nearly every day, quit the futsal team he loved, sleeps 12 hours a day, cannot concentrate and his grades are falling. He has not gained weight as expected and calls himself ‘useless’. There was no behaviour problem in primary school and no identifiable stressor or drug use.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Major depressive episode
Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder
Oppositional defiant disorder
Normal adolescent moodiness
Adjustment disorder with low mood
mcq.e: DSM-5 allows irritable mood to replace depressed mood in children and adolescents, and failure to make expected weight gain to count as the weight criterion. He has irritability, anhedonia, hypersomnia, poor concentration, weight change and worthlessness for over 2 weeks with impairment. Irritability in a teenager is easily dismissed as behaviour or normal moodiness.
w: Correct - irritable mood plus anhedonia and four other symptoms for 4 weeks meets criteria in an adolescent.
Wrong - ADHD symptoms begin before age 12 and are persistent, not a new 4-week change.
Wrong - ODD is a long-standing pattern of defiance, not a recent change with anhedonia and hypersomnia.
Wrong - anhedonia, functional decline and worthlessness are not normal adolescent moodiness.
Wrong - adjustment disorder requires an identifiable stressor, and full criteria for MDD take precedence.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old woman has 3 weeks of low mood, anhedonia, insomnia and poor concentration; PHQ-9 is 18 and she asks for an antidepressant. A year ago, for 5 days, she felt unusually elated, needed only 3 hours of sleep without tiredness, talked rapidly, started three business ventures and overspent RM8000. Colleagues noticed the change but she kept working, was never admitted and had no psychotic symptoms.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Recurrent major depressive disorder
Bipolar I disorder
Cyclothymic disorder
Persistent depressive disorder
Bipolar II disorder
mcq.e: A past episode of at least 4 days of elevated mood with reduced need for sleep and increased activity, noticeable to others but without marked impairment, admission or psychosis, is hypomania. Hypomania plus a major depressive episode is bipolar II disorder, and DSM-5 criterion E excludes MDD if there has ever been a manic or hypomanic episode. Always ask about mania before starting an antidepressant, which may trigger a switch.
w: Wrong - criterion E excludes MDD once a hypomanic or manic episode has occurred.
Wrong - bipolar I needs mania (at least 1 week, or admission, or psychosis, or marked impairment).
Wrong - cyclothymia is 2 years of subthreshold mood swings without a full depressive episode.
Wrong - persistent depressive disorder is chronic low mood for 2 years and does not explain the elated episode.
Correct - a past hypomanic episode plus a current major depressive episode is bipolar II disorder.

mcq.stem:
A 46-year-old woman has had 3 weeks of low mood and loss of enjoyment. Her energy is normal. She sleeps poorly, has a reduced appetite and has lost self-confidence, but has no guilt, no thoughts of self-harm, normal concentration and a hopeful view of the future. No symptom is intense, yet she is having considerable difficulty coping at work and at home.
Using ICD-10, how should this episode be classified?
o: Mild depressive episode
Moderate depressive episode
Severe episode without psychotic symptoms
Severe episode with psychotic symptoms
Does not yet meet criteria for an episode
mcq.e: ICD-10 grading: mild = 2 typical + 2 common symptoms; moderate = 2 typical + 3 common with considerable difficulty functioning; severe = all 3 typical + at least 4 common. She has 2 typical symptoms (low mood, loss of enjoyment) and 3 common symptoms (sleep, appetite, self-confidence) for over 2 weeks. Count carefully: energy is a typical symptom, not a common one.
w: Wrong - mild needs only 2 common symptoms; she has 3 with considerable functional difficulty.
Correct - 2 typical plus 3 common symptoms for at least 2 weeks with considerable difficulty is moderate.
Wrong - severe requires all 3 typical symptoms, and her energy is normal.
Wrong - she has no delusions or hallucinations, and severe criteria are not met anyway.
Wrong - 2 typical plus 3 common symptoms for 3 weeks clearly meets criteria.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old man is brought by his wife 9 days after his business collapsed. Over a few days he developed pervasive low mood, total loss of interest and profound exhaustion. He has stopped eating, sleeps 2 hours a night, feels worthless and guilty, cannot concentrate and sees no future. He cannot work or manage his own care. There are no delusions or hallucinations.
Using ICD-10, how should this episode be classified?
o: Acute stress reaction to the business loss
Adjustment disorder with depressed mood
Severe episode without psychotic features
Moderate depressive episode
No diagnosis until 2 weeks have passed
mcq.e: ICD-10 normally requires 2 weeks for any depressive episode, but a severe episode may be diagnosed earlier if symptoms are very severe and of very rapid onset. He has all 3 typical symptoms and at least 5 common ones and cannot function. Waiting for the 2-week mark delays urgent risk assessment and treatment.
w: Wrong - an acute stress reaction settles within hours to days; he has a full, worsening depressive syndrome.
Wrong - adjustment disorder is not used when criteria for a depressive episode are met.
Correct - very severe, rapid-onset symptoms allow a severe episode to be diagnosed before 2 weeks.
Wrong - all 3 typical plus 4 or more common symptoms with inability to function is severe, not moderate.
Wrong - ICD-10 makes an exception to the 2-week rule for very severe, rapid-onset episodes.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old woman attends a Klinik Kesihatan 7 weeks after her husband’s death. She has waves of sadness and tearfulness triggered by photographs, sleeps poorly and eats less. She still enjoys her grandchildren’s visits, laughs with friends and feels she was a good wife. She says she wishes she could be with him but has no plan or intent to end her life. PHQ-9 is 9.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review in 2 weeks
Refer urgently to psychiatry for a full assessment
Prescribe diazepam 5 mg at night for four weeks
Request TFT, FBC and a CT brain before any advice
Support, explain normal grief and arrange review
mcq.e: Grief comes in waves linked to reminders, with preserved self-esteem and capacity for pleasure; wishing to join the deceased without a plan is common. MDD shows pervasive low mood and anhedonia with worthlessness. DSM-5 asks for clinical judgement and cultural norms; here supportive care and planned review are right, watching for a depressive episode developing.
w: Wrong - antidepressants are not indicated for a normal grief reaction.
Wrong - there is no psychosis or active suicidal plan to justify urgent referral.
Wrong - benzodiazepines can impair adjustment to loss and risk dependence in the elderly.
Wrong - nothing suggests an organic cause; extensive tests are unnecessary.
Correct - preserved pleasure and self-esteem with wave-like sadness indicate normal grief; support and review.

mcq.stem:
A 47-year-old woman has had 2 months of low mood, fatigue and poor concentration; PHQ-9 is 13. She has also gained 5 kg, is constipated, feels cold all the time and her voice has become hoarse. Her skin is dry, pulse is 56/min and the ankle reflexes relax slowly.
Which investigation is most important before confirming major depressive disorder?
o: Full blood count
Fasting blood glucose
Thyroid function tests
Serum vitamin B12 and folate
Non-contrast CT brain
mcq.e: Weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, hoarseness, bradycardia and slow-relaxing reflexes point to hypothyroidism, a classic organic cause of depressive symptoms. DSM-5 criterion C excludes episodes due to another medical condition, and the CPG lists hypothyroidism among causes of non-response. Check TFT before labelling and treating MDD.
w: Wrong - anaemia can cause fatigue, but her other signs point specifically to the thyroid.
Wrong - diabetes does not explain cold intolerance, hoarseness and slow reflexes.
Correct - her features suggest hypothyroidism, a reversible cause that must be excluded.
Wrong - B12 deficiency causes neuropathy and anaemia rather than this picture.
Wrong - there are no focal neurological signs to justify neuroimaging.

mcq.stem:
A 60-year-old man is brought by his son after 5 weeks of severe low mood, total loss of interest, no energy, insomnia and refusal of most meals. He is convinced that his intestines are rotting because he is being punished for his sins, and hears a voice telling him he is worthless. He has no previous psychiatric history or manic episodes and is alert and oriented.
How should this presentation be classified?
o: Severe depressive episode with psychotic symptoms
Schizophrenia with prominent negative symptoms
Delusional disorder of the somatic type
Schizoaffective disorder, depressive type
Moderate depressive episode with somatic syndrome
mcq.e: Mood-congruent delusions (guilt, nihilistic bodily decay) and derogatory voices arising within a severe depressive episode indicate psychotic depression. The mental state examination must assess psychotic symptoms and risk, because psychotic depression needs urgent psychiatric referral. Criterion D excludes primary psychotic disorders, which are not supported when psychosis appears only during the mood episode.
w: Correct - mood-congruent delusions and hallucinations within a severe depressive episode mean psychotic depression.
Wrong - schizophrenia needs psychosis outside mood episodes; his psychosis is mood-congruent and recent.
Wrong - delusional disorder lacks a full depressive syndrome and prominent hallucinations.
Wrong - schizoaffective disorder requires psychosis persisting at least 2 weeks without mood symptoms.
Wrong - psychotic symptoms make the episode severe, not moderate.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old divorced, unemployed man with major depressive disorder scores 22 on the PHQ-9 at a Klinik Kesihatan. You carry out a suicide risk assessment.
Which finding indicates the highest immediate suicide risk?
o: He sometimes wishes he could sleep and never wake up
He feels guilty about being a burden to his children
He wakes at 4 a.m. daily and cannot get back to sleep
He has stockpiled his tablets and chosen a date
He has lost 6 kg and stopped attending the mosque
mcq.e: Risk rises steeply from passive death wishes to active ideation, then a specific plan, preparation (gathering means) and a chosen time. A plan with access to means signals high immediate risk and needs same-day urgent psychiatric referral with the means removed. Demographic factors (male, divorced, unemployed) add to risk but are less immediate.
w: Wrong - a passive death wish needs exploring but is lower risk than an active plan.
Wrong - perceived burdensomeness is a risk factor but not as immediate as a prepared plan.
Wrong - early morning waking indicates severity of depression, not imminent suicide.
Correct - a specific plan, gathered means and a chosen date indicate high immediate risk.
Wrong - weight loss and social withdrawal reflect severity, not imminence of suicide.

mcq.stem:
A 44-year-old clerk says she has ‘always been down’ for about 3 years. Most days she feels low, eats poorly, tires easily and has low self-esteem, but she has never had 2 weeks with five or more depressive symptoms and has never felt well for more than a month at a time. She keeps working, though life feels joyless. There is no history of elevated mood.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Major depressive disorder, recurrent
Persistent depressive disorder
Cyclothymic disorder
Generalised anxiety disorder
Adjustment disorder with depressed mood
mcq.e: Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) is depressed mood on most days for at least 2 years in adults, with at least 2 other symptoms and no symptom-free period over 2 months. It is milder but chronic, and full MDD criteria are never met here. It still responds to treatment and is a risk factor for later major depression.
w: Wrong - she has never met full MDD criteria of five symptoms for 2 weeks.
Correct - chronic low mood for more than 2 years with two or more symptoms is persistent depressive disorder.
Wrong - cyclothymia involves alternating hypomanic and depressive symptoms; she has never had elevated mood.
Wrong - GAD is centred on excessive worry, not persistent low mood.
Wrong - adjustment disorder follows a stressor and resolves within 6 months of it ending.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old woman attends her 6-week postnatal check at a Klinik Kesihatan. When asked the two Whooley questions, she answers ‘yes’ to both: she has felt down most days and has lost interest in things she used to enjoy. She denies thoughts of self-harm. The baby is feeding and growing well.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review her in 2 weeks
Reassure her that this is the baby blues and review in 1 month
Complete the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale at this visit
Refer her urgently to the hospital psychiatric clinic this week
Repeat the Whooley questions at her next routine clinic visit
mcq.e: Perinatal depression is screened in two stages: a brief tool first (PHQ-2 or Whooley questions), then the EPDS if the brief screen is positive. A positive brief screen is not a diagnosis, so it does not justify drug treatment or urgent referral on its own. Baby blues settle by about 2 weeks, so symptoms at 6 weeks cannot be dismissed as blues.
w: Wrong - a positive brief screen needs further assessment (EPDS, then DSM-5 interview) before any drug is started.
Wrong - baby blues peak around days 3–5 and resolve by 2 weeks; symptoms at 6 weeks need assessment.
Correct - a positive PHQ-2/Whooley screen is followed by the EPDS as the second stage of screening.
Wrong - there are no suicidal thoughts or psychotic features, so urgent referral is not yet indicated.
Wrong - deferring a positive screen delays the diagnosis and treatment of possible postnatal depression.

mcq.stem:
A 31-year-old woman, 5 weeks postpartum, completes the Malay version of the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale at a Klinik Kesihatan. Her total score is 9. On item 10 (‘The thought of harming myself has occurred to me’) she ticks ‘Hardly ever’.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Assess her suicide risk in detail during this visit
Reassure her, as the total score is below the cut-off
Repeat the EPDS in 2 weeks before taking any action
Start fluoxetine, as her total score shows depression
Refer her to a postnatal exercise and peer support group
mcq.e: The EPDS is scored out of 30 and the Malay-version cut-off is 12 or more, but any score above 0 on item 10 triggers a suicide risk assessment regardless of the total. A low total score is therefore not reassuring when item 10 is positive. The trap is to read the total score only.
w: Correct - any score above 0 on item 10 means suicide risk must be assessed now, whatever the total score.
Wrong - a total of 9 is below the cut-off of 12, but a positive item 10 cannot be ignored.
Wrong - possible suicidal thoughts must be assessed today, not deferred for 2 weeks.
Wrong - a total of 9 is below the Malay EPDS cut-off and the EPDS is a screen, not a diagnosis.
Wrong - support groups help, but they do not replace an immediate suicide risk assessment.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old woman is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan by her husband on day 6 after delivering her first baby. She has hardly slept for three nights, is restless and confused, laughs and cries in quick succession, and insists the baby has been swapped for a demon. Her mother has bipolar disorder. Temperature is 36.8 °C and capillary glucose is normal.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure the family that this is the baby blues and review in a week
Start sertraline and arrange review at the clinic in 1 week
Arrange outpatient CBT with daily home visits by the nurse
Prescribe a hypnotic for 3 nights and then review her sleep
Arrange same-day admission under the psychiatric team
mcq.e: Abrupt onset within the first 2 weeks postpartum of insomnia, confusion, labile mood and delusions about the baby is postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric emergency with risk of suicide and infanticide. A personal or family history of bipolar disorder is the main risk factor. Management is same-day admission, and the mother should not be left alone with the baby.
w: Wrong - baby blues cause tearfulness and lability but never delusions or confusion.
Wrong - an antidepressant alone may worsen a bipolar-spectrum psychosis and outpatient review is unsafe.
Wrong - psychotherapy is for mild-to-moderate depression, not acute psychosis with risk to the infant.
Wrong - sedation at home does not address the psychosis or the risk to mother and baby.
Correct - postpartum psychosis needs emergency psychiatric admission, ideally in a mother-and-baby setting.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old woman is reviewed at home by a community nurse on day 4 after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. She cries easily, feels overwhelmed and irritable, and her mood swings within the day. She sleeps whenever the baby sleeps, is feeding well, is bonding warmly with the baby and denies thoughts of harm.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Postnatal depression
Postpartum ‘baby’ blues
Postpartum psychosis
Adjustment disorder with anxiety
Postpartum thyroiditis
mcq.e: Baby blues affect up to 80% of mothers, peak at days 3–5 and resolve by 2 weeks; mood is labile and tearful but functioning and bonding are preserved. Postnatal depression needs DSM-5 symptoms for at least 2 weeks with impaired functioning. Management is reassurance, support and review to make sure symptoms settle.
w: Wrong - postnatal depression needs symptoms for at least 2 weeks with impaired functioning.
Correct - transient tearfulness and labile mood on days 3–5 with preserved functioning is the baby blues.
Wrong - there is no confusion, delusions or hallucinations.
Wrong - transient mood lability in the first week after birth is expected and best explained by the blues.
Wrong - postpartum thyroiditis usually appears from 1–4 months with thyrotoxic then hypothyroid features.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old woman, 3 months postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding, has had low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep and guilt for 6 weeks. Her EPDS is 18 with item 10 scored 0, and a clinical interview confirms a moderate-to-severe depressive episode. She has no history of bipolar disorder and, after discussion, chooses medication.
Which antidepressant is most appropriate?
o: Doxepin
Fluoxetine
Citalopram
Sertraline
Venlafaxine
mcq.e: Sertraline is the preferred antidepressant in breastfeeding because very little passes into breast milk and it has the most safety data. Fluoxetine (long half-life metabolite) and citalopram give higher infant levels, and doxepin has caused infant sedation and respiratory depression. Moderate-to-severe perinatal depression warrants an antidepressant after a risk–benefit discussion.
w: Wrong - doxepin has been linked to infant sedation and respiratory depression and should be avoided.
Wrong - fluoxetine and its active metabolite have long half-lives and accumulate in the infant.
Wrong - citalopram reaches higher infant levels than sertraline.
Correct - sertraline has low milk transfer and the most reassuring breastfeeding data.
Wrong - venlafaxine gives relatively high infant exposure and has fewer safety data than sertraline.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old widower attends a Klinik Kesihatan with constipation, tiredness, poor appetite and a 3 kg weight loss since his wife died 10 months ago. He moves and speaks slowly, says his memory is ‘useless’, and feels his health is poor. Examination, FBC, TFT and fasting glucose are normal.
Which screening tool is most appropriate to assess his main problem?
o: Mini-Mental State Examination
AD8 informant questionnaire
Confusion Assessment Method
Geriatric Depression Scale
Abbreviated Mental Test
mcq.e: Late-life depression often presents with somatic complaints (constipation, fatigue, weight loss), psychomotor retardation, poor perceived health and subjective memory complaints rather than reported sadness. The Geriatric Depression Scale is the most widely used self-rating scale for the elderly. Cognitive tools may be needed later, but the leading problem here is depression after bereavement.
w: Wrong - the MMSE screens cognition; it does not measure depressive symptoms.
Wrong - the AD8 asks an informant about cognitive change, not mood.
Wrong - the CAM screens for delirium, and he has no acute fluctuating confusion.
Correct - the Geriatric Depression Scale is the standard depression screen in older adults.
Wrong - the Abbreviated Mental Test is a brief cognitive screen, not a mood scale.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old unmarried primigravida at 14 weeks attends a Klinik Kesihatan booking visit. The pregnancy was unplanned, her partner drinks heavily and has slapped her twice, and she has felt low with poor sleep for 4 weeks. Her EPDS is 14 with item 10 scored 0, and interview confirms a mild-to-moderate depressive episode. She feels safe staying with her sister.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Start paroxetine 20 mg daily and review her in 4 weeks
Arrange psychotherapy and address the partner violence
Reassure her that low mood is normal in early pregnancy
Admit her to the psychiatric ward for close monitoring
Defer further assessment until the 6-week postnatal check
mcq.e: Unplanned pregnancy, being unmarried and young, and intimate partner violence are risk factors for perinatal depression. Mild-to-moderate perinatal depression is treated first with psychosocial support and psychotherapy, and the violence must be addressed (safety planning, OSCC/social welfare links). Paroxetine is avoided in the first trimester because of cardiac malformation risk.
w: Wrong - drugs are not first line for mild-to-moderate perinatal depression, and paroxetine is avoided in the first trimester.
Correct - psychotherapy plus psychosocial support and action on the intimate partner violence is first line.
Wrong - a confirmed depressive episode with risk factors is not normal and needs treatment.
Wrong - there is no suicidal risk, psychosis or inability to self-care, so admission is not indicated.
