Wrong - untreated antenatal depression strongly predicts postnatal depression and harms mother and baby.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old man with moderate major depressive disorder started fluoxetine 20 mg daily 3 weeks ago at a Klinik Kesihatan. He takes it every day, has only mild nausea, and his PHQ-9 has barely changed (17 to 16). He has no suicidal ideas or psychotic symptoms.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Switch to sertraline 50 mg daily from tomorrow
Add risperidone as augmentation and review in 4 weeks
Continue 20 mg as a response takes at least 12 weeks
Refer to psychiatry for treatment-resistant depression
Increase fluoxetine to 40 mg daily and review in 2 weeks
mcq.e: Response is assessed after 2–4 weeks; if there is none, the first step in the Malaysian CPG algorithm is to optimise the dose as tolerated and reassess after 2 weeks. Switching class, combining or augmenting is reserved for failure after optimisation. Treatment resistance cannot be declared after one under-dosed trial.
w: Wrong - switching comes only after the dose has been optimised without adequate response.
Wrong - augmentation with an atypical antipsychotic is a later strategy, usually with specialist input.
Wrong - lack of any response by 2–4 weeks predicts poor response, so waiting passively is not advised.
Wrong - one sub-optimally dosed antidepressant trial is not treatment-resistant depression.
Correct - no response after 2–4 weeks: titrate the dose as tolerated and reassess after 2 weeks.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old teacher had her first episode of moderate major depressive disorder. She has been in full remission for 2 months on sertraline 100 mg daily and has no residual symptoms. She asks when she can stop the medication.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Continue for 6–9 months after remission, then taper
Stop now, since she has been in remission for 2 months
Continue for 4 more weeks and then stop it abruptly
Continue it lifelong, as depression always recurs
Continue for at least 5 years, then reduce slowly
mcq.e: The Malaysian MDD CPG advises continuing the antidepressant for 6–9 months after the onset of remission to prevent relapse, extending to 2 years or more when the risk of relapse or recurrence is high. Stopping is done by tapering to avoid discontinuation symptoms. A first, uncomplicated episode does not need lifelong treatment.
w: Correct - continuation for 6–9 months after remission, then gradual tapering, follows the CPG.
Wrong - stopping 2 months into remission carries a high risk of relapse.
Wrong - the duration is too short and abrupt stopping causes discontinuation symptoms.
Wrong - lifelong treatment is not needed after a single uncomplicated episode.
Wrong - 2 years or more is for high relapse risk; 5 years is not the standard for a first episode.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old man has had little response to adequate doses of escitalopram and then venlafaxine, taken as prescribed (pharmacy records confirm). His sister mentions that last year he went a week with almost no sleep, spent his savings on a car and talked non-stop about business plans. TFT and FBC are normal and he does not use drugs.
What is the most likely reason for his poor response?
o: Undiagnosed hypothyroidism
Poor adherence to treatment
Undiagnosed bipolar disorder
Comorbid substance misuse
Antidepressant discontinuation
mcq.e: When depression fails to respond, the CPG asks you to reconsider the diagnosis, and the classic miss is bipolar disorder. A past week of reduced need for sleep, overspending and pressured speech suggests a manic or hypomanic episode. Antidepressant monotherapy can be ineffective or trigger switching, so he needs psychiatric referral for mood stabiliser treatment.
w: Wrong - his thyroid function is normal.
Wrong - pharmacy records confirm he takes his medication.
Correct - a previous episode of decreased sleep, overspending and pressured talk points to missed bipolar disorder.
Wrong - he does not use drugs or alcohol.
Wrong - he is taking his medication regularly, so there are no discontinuation effects to explain non-response.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old divorced man with major depressive disorder attends a Klinik Kesihatan. He says he has written a will, bought charcoal and plans to end his life in his flat this weekend. He lives alone, drinks most nights and sees no reason to go on. There are no psychotic symptoms.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start fluoxetine and review him again in 1 week
Give a crisis hotline number and review tomorrow
Refer him to the psychiatric clinic within 2 weeks
Arrange immediate admission with a safe escort
Ask him to sign a no-suicide contract and go home
mcq.e: An active suicidal plan with preparation (will, method obtained, date) is high risk of harm to self and is a criterion for admission, not just referral. He should not be left alone and must be escorted to hospital; the Mental Health Act 2001 can be used if he refuses. Living alone, alcohol and male sex add to the risk.
w: Wrong - an antidepressant takes weeks to act and does nothing for the immediate risk this weekend.
Wrong - a hotline does not make a man with a prepared plan safe overnight.
Wrong - active suicidal intent with a plan needs same-day admission, not an outpatient appointment.
Correct - risk of harm to self with a prepared plan is an admission criterion; escort him and do not leave him alone.
Wrong - no-suicide contracts are not protective and must never replace risk management.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old woman attends a Klinik Kesihatan with low mood, anhedonia and poor sleep for 3 weeks. Nine months ago she had a depressive episode that remitted on sertraline, which she stopped herself after 3 months. Her PHQ-9 is 14, she denies suicidal thoughts and has no psychotic symptoms. Symptoms began after stress at work; she also has treated hypertension and had nausea when she first took sertraline.
Which feature is an indication for referral to a psychiatrist?
o: Her PHQ-9 score of 14 at this visit
A new episode within a year of the last
Her coexisting treated hypertension
Onset of symptoms after stress at work
Nausea when she first took sertraline
mcq.e: Referral criteria for MDD in the slides include a recurrent episode within one year, uncertainty about the diagnosis, attempted suicide or active suicidal ideas, psychotic symptoms, treatment failure, severe agitation, self-neglect and clinical deterioration. A moderate PHQ-9, a stressful trigger, a comorbidity or a transient side effect can all be managed in primary care. Early relapse after stopping treatment also signals the need for longer maintenance.
w: Wrong - a PHQ-9 of 14 is moderate depression, which can be managed in primary care.
Correct - a recurrent episode within one year is a listed criterion for psychiatric referral.
Wrong - well-controlled hypertension is not a reason for psychiatric referral.
Wrong - a psychosocial trigger is common and does not by itself need specialist care.
Wrong - early nausea on SSRIs is common and transient and is not a referral criterion.

mcq.stem:
A 78-year-old woman weighing 42 kg was started on escitalopram 10 mg daily 3 weeks ago for depression. She also takes hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. Her daughter brings her to a Klinik Kesihatan because over 2 days she has become nauseated, drowsy, confused and unsteady. She is afebrile and has no focal neurological signs.
Which investigation is most likely to reveal the cause?
o: Serum electrolytes
Urine FEME
CT brain
Thyroid function test
Serum vitamin B12
mcq.e: SSRIs, SNRIs, mirtazapine and TCAs can cause hyponatraemia through SIADH, usually in the first weeks of treatment. High-risk groups are the elderly, those with low body weight, thiazide or carbamazepine users and anyone with previous antidepressant-induced hyponatraemia; sodium should be checked at baseline and about 1 month. Nausea, confusion and unsteadiness soon after starting an SSRI in this patient point to low sodium.
w: Correct - SSRI plus thiazide in a frail elderly woman makes SIADH-related hyponatraemia the likely cause.
Wrong - infection can cause delirium, but she is afebrile and the drug timing points to hyponatraemia.
Wrong - there are no focal signs or head injury; imaging is not the first test here.
Wrong - hypothyroidism develops slowly and does not explain a 2-day decline after a new drug.
Wrong - B12 deficiency causes gradual cognitive and neurological change, not a 2-day confusional state.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man with major depressive disorder was started on agomelatine 25 mg at night 6 weeks ago and is improving. His baseline liver function was normal, but his ALT is now four times the upper limit of normal. He is asymptomatic, not jaundiced and does not drink alcohol.
What is the most appropriate action?
o: Continue it and repeat the LFT at 12 weeks as scheduled
Halve the dose and recheck the LFT in 2 weeks
Continue it, as rises below 5 times normal are acceptable
Add a second antidepressant and keep the same dose
Stop agomelatine and repeat the LFT until normal
mcq.e: Agomelatine needs liver function tests at baseline and at 3, 6, 12 and 24 weeks, and after dose increases. Treatment must be discontinued if transaminases exceed three times the upper limit of normal, even without symptoms. An alternative antidepressant can then be chosen once the LFT is followed up.
w: Wrong - an ALT above 3 times normal requires stopping the drug now, not waiting.
Wrong - dose reduction is not the recommended response to hepatotoxicity.
Wrong - the threshold for stopping agomelatine is 3 times the upper limit of normal, not 5.
Wrong - adding another drug while continuing a hepatotoxic one is unsafe.
Correct - transaminases above 3 times the upper limit of normal mean agomelatine must be discontinued.

mcq.stem:
A 33-year-old woman stopped her paroxetine 20 mg abruptly 3 days ago because she felt well after 10 months of treatment. She now has dizziness, ‘electric shock’ sensations in her head, nausea, vivid dreams and irritability. Her mood has remained good and she has no vertigo on head movement.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Explain this is a relapse and double her usual dose
Start diazepam 5 mg three times daily for a week
Restart paroxetine, then taper it slowly over weeks
Refer her to an addiction service for dependence
Start betahistine and arrange an ENT clinic review
mcq.e: Abrupt cessation of a short half-life antidepressant such as paroxetine or venlafaxine commonly causes discontinuation syndrome within a few days: dizziness, shock-like sensations, flu-like symptoms, sleep disturbance and irritability. Reinstating the drug relieves symptoms within a day or so, after which it is tapered over at least 4 weeks. It is not addiction and not a relapse, as her mood is good.
w: Wrong - her mood is good; these are discontinuation symptoms, not a relapse of depression.
Wrong - benzodiazepines do not treat discontinuation syndrome and add dependence risk.
Correct - reinstate paroxetine and taper it gradually to prevent discontinuation symptoms.
Wrong - discontinuation syndrome is not dependence or addiction.
Wrong - there is no vestibular disorder; the dizziness is from abrupt stopping of paroxetine.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old man has attended a Klinik Kesihatan many times over the past year, convinced he has HIV or lymphoma. He has no symptoms, examination is normal and repeated HIV, FBC and ultrasound results are normal. He checks his neck for lumps every day and is reassured for only a few days. He accepts that he might be worrying too much.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Illness anxiety disorder
Somatic symptom disorder
Generalised anxiety disorder
Factitious disorder
Delusional disorder, somatic type
mcq.e: Illness anxiety disorder is preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness for at least 6 months with minimal or no somatic symptoms, plus checking or avoidance behaviour. Somatic symptom disorder requires prominent distressing symptoms. Because he can accept that his fear may be excessive, the belief is not delusional.
w: Correct - health preoccupation for at least 6 months with no symptoms and repeated checking is illness anxiety disorder.
Wrong - somatic symptom disorder needs distressing somatic symptoms, and he has none.
Wrong - GAD involves worry across many areas of life, not a single fixed illness fear.
Wrong - nothing suggests he is faking or inducing illness to take on the sick role.
Wrong - the belief is not fixed; he accepts he might be worrying too much.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old clerk has had widespread joint pain, fatigue and palpitations for 2 years. Mild knee osteoarthritis was confirmed on X-ray, and ECG, FBC and TFT are normal. She spends hours each day reading about serious diseases, believes her symptoms mean something is being missed, has seen five doctors this year and has stopped working. She is not seeking compensation.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Illness anxiety disorder
Conversion disorder
Malingering
Panic disorder
Somatic symptom disorder
mcq.e: Somatic symptom disorder is one or more distressing somatic symptoms with excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviours about them (disproportionate concern about seriousness, persistently high health anxiety, or excessive time and energy devoted to symptoms). Symptoms may occur with or without an identified medical disease, so her osteoarthritis does not exclude the diagnosis. The course is usually persistent, although individual symptoms change.
w: Wrong - illness anxiety disorder has minimal or no symptoms, whereas her symptoms are prominent.
Wrong - conversion disorder involves neurological symptoms incompatible with disease, such as weakness or seizures.
Wrong - she is not faking symptoms and has no external incentive.
Wrong - panic disorder involves recurrent discrete surges of fear peaking within minutes.
Correct - distressing symptoms with excessive time, anxiety and behaviour around them is somatic symptom disorder.

mcq.stem:
A 39-year-old woman with somatic symptom disorder attends a Klinik Kesihatan almost weekly with changing complaints of headache, abdominal pain and tiredness. Examination and investigations over the past year have been normal, and she has no red-flag features. Each visit is with a different doctor and usually ends with another blood test.
What is the most appropriate approach to her care?
o: Repeat the full blood panel at each visit to reassure her
Refer her to whichever specialist matches each new symptom
Book regular brief reviews with one named doctor
Tell her the symptoms are imaginary and stop follow-up
Prescribe tramadol for her pains to use as needed
mcq.e: Frequent attenders with medically unexplained symptoms do best with continuity: regular, brief, scheduled visits with one doctor rather than symptom-driven visits, a brief examination each time, and investigations or referrals only for clear indications. The symptoms are acknowledged as real while the focus shifts to function and coping, with CBT and treatment of comorbid depression or anxiety. Repeated tests and referrals reinforce illness behaviour.
w: Wrong - repeated normal tests reassure only briefly and reinforce health anxiety.
Wrong - multiple referrals increase iatrogenic harm and cost without benefit.
Correct - scheduled, time-limited visits with one doctor reduce symptom-driven attendance and investigations.
Wrong - the symptoms are real to her; dismissing them damages trust and leads to doctor shopping.
Wrong - opioids carry dependence risk and do not help somatic symptom disorder.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old staff nurse has had four admissions for hypoglycaemia over 6 months. She is not diabetic. During the latest episode, glucose was 1.9 mmol/L with a very high serum insulin and a suppressed C-peptide. She has no financial problems, is not seeking leave or compensation and appears to welcome hospital admission.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Insulinoma
Malingering
Somatic symptom disorder
Factitious disorder
Conversion disorder
mcq.e: High insulin with suppressed C-peptide means exogenous insulin, so the hypoglycaemia is self-induced. Deliberately produced illness without external reward, to assume the sick role, is factitious disorder. Malingering is also deliberate but is driven by an external incentive such as money, leave or drugs.
w: Wrong - an insulinoma secretes endogenous insulin, so C-peptide would be high, not suppressed.
Wrong - malingering requires an external incentive, and she has none.
Wrong - in somatic symptom disorder the symptoms are not intentionally produced.
Correct - intentionally induced illness with no external reward, seeking the sick role, is factitious disorder.
Wrong - conversion disorder causes unintentional neurological symptoms, not biochemical hypoglycaemia.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man has had somatic symptom disorder for years with recurrent abdominal pain; gastroscopy and colonoscopy 5 years ago were normal. Over 3 months he has developed looser stools, 5 kg weight loss and fatigue. Hb is 9.8 g/dL with a low MCV. He is on sertraline and attends scheduled monthly reviews.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure him that this is his usual pattern of symptoms
Refer him for an urgent colonoscopy within 2 weeks
Increase his sertraline dose and review in 4 weeks
Book more frequent scheduled visits for support
Refer him to a psychologist for more sessions of CBT
mcq.e: Patients with somatic symptom disorder can still develop organic disease. A new or changed symptom pattern, especially after 50, with weight loss and objective abnormalities such as iron-deficiency anaemia, is a red flag that needs fresh investigation. Here change in bowel habit with microcytic anaemia requires urgent assessment for colorectal cancer.
w: Wrong - new symptoms with weight loss and anaemia must not be attributed to his known disorder.
Correct - change in bowel habit, weight loss and iron-deficiency anaemia after 50 needs urgent colonoscopy.
Wrong - altering psychiatric treatment ignores objective red flags.
Wrong - scheduled visits suit stable unexplained symptoms, not new objective abnormalities.
Wrong - CBT does not address possible colorectal cancer.

mcq.stem:
An 82-year-old woman with mild forgetfulness, previously independent in self-care, is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan because over 2 days she has become confused, drowsy in the day and agitated at night. She cannot keep her attention on the conversation or name the months backwards. Temperature is 37.9 °C and urine dipstick is positive for nitrites and leucocytes.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Rapid progression of Alzheimer disease
Delirium due to an acute precipitant
Dementia with Lewy bodies
Depression with cognitive impairment
Stepwise vascular dementia
mcq.e: Acute onset over hours to days, fluctuating course, inattention and altered alertness with a clear precipitant (here a urinary tract infection) define delirium. Pre-existing cognitive impairment is the strongest risk factor, so ‘acute on chronic’ confusion is common. Delirium is usually reversible and the precipitant must be treated; screen with the Confusion Assessment Method.
w: Wrong - Alzheimer disease progresses over months to years, not over 2 days.
Correct - acute fluctuating confusion with inattention and an infection is delirium.
Wrong - Lewy body dementia fluctuates, but it develops gradually and is not triggered by a fever.
Wrong - depression does not cause acute drowsiness, inattention and fever-linked confusion.
Wrong - stepwise vascular decline follows strokes and shows focal signs, not febrile confusion.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old retired teacher attends a Klinik Kesihatan with her husband. Since their son died 3 months ago she complains that her memory is ‘terrible’. She wakes early, has lost her appetite and answers many MMSE items with ‘I don’t know’ after little effort, scoring 22. Before the bereavement she was managing well.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start donepezil 5 mg at night and review in 6 weeks
Request an MRI brain before any further assessment
Reassure her that this is normal ageing after a loss
Assess her mood with the GDS and treat depression
Refer to the memory clinic for amyloid PET imaging
mcq.e: Subacute onset after a loss, complaints of poor memory, ‘don’t know’ answers with poor effort and biological symptoms of depression suggest depression with cognitive impairment (pseudodementia). People with dementia tend to minimise deficits and give near-miss answers. Screen with the Geriatric Depression Scale and treat the depression, then reassess cognition, as depression can also herald dementia.
w: Wrong - starting a cholinesterase inhibitor before addressing obvious depression treats the wrong condition.
Wrong - imaging may be needed later, but the clinical picture points first to depression.
Wrong - low mood with biological symptoms and cognitive complaints is not normal ageing.
Correct - the picture suggests depressive pseudodementia, so assess and treat mood, then reassess cognition.
Wrong - amyloid imaging is a specialist tool and is not the next step here.

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin for 15 years has had gradually worsening memory and low mood for a year. He has numbness of both feet, reduced vibration sense and an unsteady gait. FBC shows Hb 11.2 g/dL with MCV 108 fL. His thyroid function last month was normal.
Which investigation is most likely to reveal a reversible cause?
o: Serum vitamin B12
Serum calcium
Thyroid function test
Syphilis serology
HbA1c
mcq.e: Every patient with new cognitive decline needs a reversible-cause screen (FBC, renal and liver function, glucose, calcium, TFT, B12, folate and syphilis serology, with HIV if at risk). Long-term metformin reduces B12 absorption, and the combination of cognitive change, macrocytosis and dorsal column signs points to B12 deficiency. Treating it can halt or partly reverse the decline.
w: Correct - long-term metformin, macrocytosis and neuropathy with cognitive decline point to B12 deficiency.
Wrong - hypercalcaemia causes confusion, but nothing here explains macrocytosis or neuropathy.
Wrong - his thyroid function was normal last month.
Wrong - neurosyphilis is a screened mimic, but metformin use and macrocytosis favour B12 deficiency.
Wrong - HbA1c measures glycaemic control and does not explain his cognitive decline.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old man has become slow and forgetful over 8 months. He walks with a broad-based, shuffling gait as if his feet are stuck to the floor, and has developed urgency with urinary incontinence. There is no tremor or rigidity in the arms and no history of stroke. Blood tests including B12 and TFT are normal.
Which investigation should be arranged next?
o: Electroencephalogram
Urodynamic studies
Nerve conduction study
Lumbar puncture for CSF
Non-contrast CT brain
mcq.e: Gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline form the triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus, a potentially reversible dementia mimic that is excluded by imaging. CT or MRI shows ventricles enlarged out of proportion to atrophy. Confirmed cases are referred to neurosurgery for a CSF tap test and possible ventriculoperitoneal shunting.
w: Wrong - EEG helps in suspected Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease or seizures, not this triad.
Wrong - urodynamics investigate the bladder alone and miss the cause of the triad.
Wrong - nerve conduction studies assess neuropathy; the gait here is not neuropathic.
Wrong - a CSF tap test may follow, but imaging must come first to show the ventriculomegaly.
Correct - gait apraxia, incontinence and cognitive decline suggest normal pressure hydrocephalus, shown on brain imaging.

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old woman attends a Klinik Kesihatan worried about her memory. Over a year she has had trouble recalling names and now relies on lists and a calendar. She still manages her own finances, cooking, medication and travel without help. Her MoCA score is 23/30 after education adjustment, and blood tests are normal. There is no low mood.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Age-associated memory change
Mild major neurocognitive disorder
Mild cognitive impairment
Depressive pseudodementia
Moderate major neurocognitive disorder
mcq.e: In DSM-5, the key difference between mild cognitive impairment (mild neurocognitive disorder) and dementia (major neurocognitive disorder) is function. Modest decline with independence in everyday activities, even if compensatory strategies such as lists are used, is MCI. Her MoCA below 26 shows the decline is more than normal ageing, and she should be reviewed regularly as some people progress to dementia.
w: Wrong - a MoCA of 23 is below the normal cut-off of 26, so this is more than normal ageing.
Wrong - dementia requires deficits that interfere with independence in everyday activities.
Correct - objective modest decline with preserved independence in daily activities is mild cognitive impairment.
Wrong - she has no low mood or depressive features.
Wrong - moderate dementia means needing help with basic activities such as dressing and feeding.

mcq.stem:
A 76-year-old man has had insidious memory decline over 2 years. He now needs help with his finances and shopping but dresses, eats and bathes independently. MMSE is 22/30, the reversible-cause screen is normal and CT brain shows generalised atrophy only. Pulse is 74/min and regular, and he has no asthma or peptic ulcer.
Which drug is most appropriate for his cognitive symptoms?
o: Memantine
Risperidone
Donepezil
Ginkgo biloba
High-dose vitamin E
mcq.e: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) increase acetylcholine and are indicated for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease, alongside non-drug measures such as cognitive stimulation and physical activity. Memantine, an NMDA receptor antagonist, is used in moderate-to-severe disease alone or with an AChEI. Check the pulse first because AChEIs can cause bradycardia.
w: Wrong - memantine is indicated for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease.
Wrong - antipsychotics are only for severe, dangerous BPSD and do not treat cognition.
Correct - an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor is first-line drug treatment for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease.
Wrong - ginkgo biloba has no convincing evidence of benefit and may raise bleeding risk.
Wrong - high-dose vitamin E is not recommended to treat cognitive symptoms.

mcq.stem:
A 79-year-old woman with Alzheimer disease has taken donepezil 10 mg daily for 4 months. She also takes bisoprolol for hypertension. Her daughter reports two episodes of sudden collapse with brief loss of consciousness this week. Her pulse is 44/min and regular, BP 118/70 mmHg lying and 114/68 mmHg standing.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue donepezil and add a pill organiser for adherence
Switch donepezil to the rivastigmine patch at once
Start fludrocortisone for orthostatic hypotension
Advise more fluids, as these are vasovagal faints
Withhold donepezil and arrange an urgent ECG
mcq.e: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors increase vagal tone and can cause bradycardia, heart block and syncope, especially with beta-blockers or conduction disease. Syncope with a pulse of 44 needs the drug withheld and an urgent ECG, with referral if heart block is found. There is no significant postural drop, so orthostatic hypotension is not the explanation.
w: Wrong - continuing the drug risks further syncope and injury.
Wrong - rivastigmine is also a cholinesterase inhibitor and causes the same bradycardia.
Wrong - her BP drop on standing is minimal, so this is not orthostatic hypotension.
Wrong - a pulse of 44 with syncope on donepezil and bisoprolol is not a simple faint.
Correct - cholinergic bradycardia with syncope: stop donepezil and do an urgent ECG to look for heart block.

mcq.stem:
An 84-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer disease, cared for at home by his daughter, has for 3 days been shouting, restless at night and has hit out at her during washing. He has not opened his bowels for 6 days and grimaces when his right hip is moved. He is afebrile and there are no hallucinations or delusions.
What is the most appropriate first step?
o: Look for and treat pain, constipation and infection
Start risperidone 0.5 mg at night for the agitation
Start haloperidol 5 mg as needed when he is aggressive
Prescribe diazepam 5 mg to calm him in the evenings
Admit him to a psychiatric ward for behavioural control
mcq.e: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia are often a sign of an unmet need such as pain, constipation, infection, urinary retention or sensory loss. The first step is to address these causes and use psychosocial and environmental measures with carer education. Antipsychotics are reserved for severe or dangerous symptoms, short term, because of stroke risk, sedation and increased mortality.
w: Correct - new agitation in dementia must first be checked for pain, constipation and infection.
Wrong - antipsychotics are reserved for severe, dangerous BPSD after causes are treated, given stroke risk.
Wrong - haloperidol carries high risk of falls, rigidity and death in dementia and ignores the likely causes.
Wrong - benzodiazepines worsen confusion and falls and do not treat the cause.
Wrong - admission is not needed when a treatable cause of agitation is evident.

mcq.stem:
An 80-year-old woman with mild Alzheimer disease, stable for a year on donepezil, has become more forgetful and muddled over 4 weeks. During that time she was started on oxybutynin for urge incontinence and chlorpheniramine for itchy skin. She is alert, afebrile and her blood tests are unchanged.
What is the most appropriate action?
o: Increase the donepezil dose to 10 mg daily
Add memantine to her current donepezil
Start low-dose quetiapine at bedtime
Stop the oxybutynin and chlorpheniramine
Refer her for an urgent MRI brain scan
mcq.e: Anticholinergic drugs such as oxybutynin, first-generation antihistamines, TCAs and hyoscine worsen cognition in dementia and directly oppose cholinesterase inhibitors. A decline that follows new anticholinergic prescriptions should prompt deprescribing and a review of anticholinergic burden before any change in dementia treatment. Non-anticholinergic alternatives can be used for the bladder and itch.
w: Wrong - raising the AChEI dose does not overcome drugs that block acetylcholine.
Wrong - adding memantine ignores the drug-induced cause of her decline.
Wrong - an antipsychotic adds sedation and risk and does not address the cause.
Correct - the new anticholinergic drugs are the likely cause of decline and should be stopped.
Wrong - the decline is clearly linked to new medicines; imaging is not the first step.

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man has had 9 months of memory and attention problems that vary markedly from day to day. He sees detailed images of children in his house, and his wife says he shouts and kicks in his sleep. Mild rigidity and slowness began around the same time as the memory problems. He has become agitated at night and his son asks for something to calm him.
Which drug is most likely to cause a severe adverse reaction in this patient?
o: Rivastigmine
Haloperidol
Donepezil
Melatonin
Paracetamol
mcq.e: Fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism that appears with or before the dementia point to dementia with Lewy bodies. These patients have severe sensitivity to antipsychotics, especially typical agents such as haloperidol, which can cause severe rigidity, falls, neuroleptic malignant syndrome and death. Cholinesterase inhibitors are helpful, and melatonin may be used for REM sleep behaviour disorder.
w: Wrong - rivastigmine is useful for cognition and hallucinations in Lewy body and Parkinson dementia.
Correct - typical antipsychotics can cause severe, sometimes fatal, sensitivity reactions in Lewy body dementia.
Wrong - donepezil is generally beneficial in Lewy body dementia.
Wrong - melatonin is a safe option for REM sleep behaviour disorder.
Wrong - paracetamol is safe and useful when pain contributes to agitation.
